limitations: The authors state only that the findings 'suggest' a protective effect and that future large-scale studies are required to confirm the benefit
They note there are no data on how long the duct should be stented
critique: Nineteen patients and three events cannot establish an effect. The nominally significant p = 0.02 comes from a 3-versus-0 comparison, and the intention-to-treat analysis the authors themselves perform is frankly negative (p = 0.3) - a result that should have been the headline rather than a mid-paper aside

Stopping early at an interim look triggered by a high event rate in the control arm is the classic route to an overestimated treatment effect; no alpha adjustment is applied, and the trial has roughly a fifth of its planned sample

The three analyses presented (per protocol excluding the failed placement, as-treated, intention-to-treat) give p = 0.05, 0.02 and 0.3 from 19 patients; reporting the most favourable as the result is selective

Single endoscopist, single centre, single operator technique - specifically en bloc snare without a submucosal cushion so as to include the sphincteric musculature - which the authors argue reduces later cannulation-related pancreatitis. The result therefore cannot be separated from one operator's method, and no learning-curve or centre-effect data exist

Patients were blinded but outcome ascertainment depended on patients reporting pain and then having enzymes checked; the endoscopist was necessarily unblinded, and whether the 24-hour telephone assessor's blinding was maintained for the stented patients who returned for fluoroscopy and stent removal is doubtful

Allocation by card from a sealed envelope without blocking or stratification produced unequal arms (11 vs 8) and a 9-year age difference between groups in a 19-patient trial; concealment by opaque envelope is weaker than central randomisation
The outcome window was only 24 hours, so delayed pancreatitis, bleeding, perforation, papillary stenosis and recurrence - the complications that matter over the longer term - were not captured at all

Electrosurgical generator changed during the study (Meditron to ERBE) and all three pancreatitis cases occurred with the ERBE device; generator is therefore confounded with time and potentially with allocation, and is not adjusted for

Pancreatitis was defined as threefold enzyme elevation with pain but enzymes were measured only in symptomatic patients, so asymptomatic hyperamylasaemia and milder events were differentially unascertained

The companion randomised trial in this depot (Lee 2016) found 18% versus 13% pancreatitis with wire-guided versus conventional papillectomy despite 100% stent success in the wire-guided arm, and the later ESGE guideline rates prophylactic stenting as moderate-quality evidence drawing on larger series - so this trial's 0% stented pancreatitis rate is almost certainly an artefact of its size
16111953.n: 19 patients enrolled and randomised (11 assigned to stent, 8 to no stent); final stent placement achieved in 10, so analysis compared 10 stented with 9 unstented patients
16111953.bottom_line: The first and still most-cited randomised trial of prophylactic pancreatic stenting after snare ampullectomy, reporting 33% versus 0% pancreatitis, but it enrolled only 19 patients, was stopped early at an interim look, and lost statistical significance on its own intention-to-treat analysis - it is a signal consistent with a protective effect rather than proof of one.

limitations: The paper carries no limitations section; the authors note instead that the optimal duration of biliary drainage has never been established and that a shorter period may not allow recovery of metabolic abnormalities while a longer one risks stent occlusion and bile-duct inflammation

They point out that four of five earlier randomised trials used percutaneous rather than endoscopic drainage and included both proximal and distal obstruction, entities now considered different diseases needing different treatment
They concede that, given the poor results with plastic stents, drainage during neoadjuvant treatment might be better achieved with metal stents
critique: The composite primary outcome counts drainage complications and surgical complications in the same tally, so a trial of whether drainage makes surgery safer is decided mainly by whether drainage itself causes harm. On the question clinicians actually ask - does jaundice at operation increase surgical risk? - the trial is null (47% vs 37%, RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.57-1.11), and that is the result buried in the secondary analysis

Plastic stents only. A 26% cholangitis rate and 30% stent-exchange rate are features of 10 Fr plastic endoprostheses left for 4-6 weeks; the trial cannot be read as evidence against short-course drainage or against self-expanding metal stents, which the authors themselves recommend for the neoadjuvant setting

Early surgery required guaranteed theatre capacity within a week at 13 hospitals; 3 patients crossed over to drainage because surgery could not be arranged in time. Outside a trial that logistic constraint is the usual reason drainage happens, so the comparison tests an idealised pathway

Noninferiority was the prespecified frame with a 10 percentage-point margin and one-sided alpha 0.05, yet the trial is universally cited as showing drainage causes harm. Converting a noninferiority design into a superiority claim post hoc, even with a nominal superiority test appended, inflates confidence in the direction of effect

The trial is a pancreatic-head trial: 92% had adenocarcinoma and site was recorded only as 'pancreatic versus periampullary' as a covariate, with no subgroup result for ampullary tumours. Ampullary cancers are typically diagnosed at lower bilirubin, are more often endoscopically accessible and are far more often resectable, so the applicability of these complication rates to ampullary disease is assumed rather than shown

Only 61% of patients ultimately had a resection and 31% had palliative bypass; the palliative subgroup showed the largest difference (55% vs 18%, p = 0.003), so the headline result is partly driven by patients who were never going to benefit from resection and in whom stenting would now be definitive therapy rather than preoperative preparation

No blinding was possible for patients or surgeons, and the primary outcome - a complication 'that prompted an additional intervention resulting in extension of stay, readmission or death' - is partly a healthcare-utilisation endpoint sensitive to unblinded clinician behaviour, even though an adjudication committee classified events blind
Baseline imbalance in sex (70% vs 52% male, p = 0.01) and BMI (24.0 vs 25.2, p = 0.03) occurred despite randomisation and is handled only by covariate adjustment
Mortality was 7% overall and did not differ between arms, but the trial had no power for this: the relative risk for death from a protocol complication was 0.48 with an interval from 0.15 to 1.51

Events were counted to 120 days after randomisation, which in the drainage arm includes a 4-6 week pre-surgical window with no equivalent exposure period in the early surgery arm - so the drainage group was observed at risk for longer before the operation, which mechanically favours early surgery on a time-unadjusted count

A 2003-2008 trial predates routine metal stenting, modern ERCP prophylaxis including rectal NSAIDs and current neoadjuvant pathways; the authors' own recommendation at the end of the paper effectively concedes that the intervention tested is no longer the intervention used
20071702.n: 202 randomised, 196 analysed (94 early surgery, 102 preoperative biliary drainage) after 6 exclusions (2 withdrew consent, 4 ineligible bilirubin); resection performed in 63 (67%) versus 57 (56%), p = 0.11
20071702.bottom_line: Routine 4-6 week preoperative plastic-stent biliary drainage before resection for pancreatic head cancer roughly doubles overall serious complications (74% vs 39%) because of stent-related cholangitis and occlusion, without reducing surgery-related complications or mortality - so early surgery is preferred when it can be arranged; the trial says nothing specific about ampullary tumours, used only plastic stents, and its null secondary result on surgical complications is the finding most often overlooked.
20071702.funding: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development, which had no access to outcome data during the trial and no role in analysis or manuscript preparation; no endoscopic equipment or stents were donated by manufacturers. Two authors disclosed lecture or consulting fees (Boston Scientific; GI Dynamics, Covidien, Johnson & Johnson).

limitations: The unadjusted primary analysis did not show a significant benefit for adjuvant chemotherapy, and the authors state explicitly that the positive multivariable result and the gemcitabine-specific result should be considered hypothesis generating

A separate survival analysis for each tumour type could not be built into the trial design because the low incidence of each would have required an unattainably large sample and timeline; the different types were combined pragmatically because presentation and surgery are the same
Intrapancreatic bile duct cancer may need to be treated as a completely separate entity, and grouping should perhaps be avoided not only for ampullary but also for more proximal bile duct cancers
There was no single central review of histological sections - only central review of pathology reports by several experienced pathologists, which the authors argue makes systematic error unlikely
The dichotomised intestinal/pancreatobiliary classification was not widely applied when the trial started
Postoperative CA19-9 had too many missing values to be retained in the final models
The survival effect of chemotherapy was modest, indicating a need for further improvement and for testing combination chemotherapy
critique: The adjustment that converts the result from negative to positive was for age, bile duct histology, poor differentiation and node positivity - and the observation arm was prognostically the worst on two of those at baseline (poorly differentiated 33% vs 22% and 19%; node positive 62% vs 60% and 54%), so the shift from HR 0.86 to 0.75 is partly correcting a randomisation imbalance. That cuts both ways, but it means the 0.75 is not an independent confirmation of the primary analysis; it is the same data with the imbalance removed, and its CI (0.57-0.98) only just excludes 1

The trial was powered on 243 deaths and 430 patients to detect a 12% absolute 5-year gain (HR 0.68) across the pooled periampullary population. It was never powered for the ampullary subgroup, and it is the ampullary subgroup that pathway documents cite. With 297 ampullary patients, 151 deaths and three arms, no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival is reported at all - the ampullary medians of 40.6/57.8/70.8 months appear without a p value

Pooling created a group in which chemotherapy appeared harmful: in the 96 bile duct patients both regimens had numerically shorter median survival than observation. Any pooled 'benefit' is therefore driven entirely by the ampullary and other patients, and the trial's own discussion concedes bile duct cancer may be a separate entity - which is an argument that the pooled primary analysis answered the wrong question

The subtype analysis that the field quotes as evidence that subtype does not predict chemotherapy response is grossly underpowered: 162 of 297 ampullary tumours (55%) were indeterminate, leaving 80 intestinal and 46 pancreatobiliary split across three treatment arms - roughly 15-27 patients per subtype-by-arm cell. No interaction test, no numbers per cell and no power calculation are given, and 'tests of heterogeneity within pathological subgroups did not reveal any significant findings' is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence

Subtype was assigned from central review of pathology reports, not of slides; the same institutional tradition that produced these categories has since shown that slide-based subtyping has only fair reproducibility and that 40% of ampullary carcinomas are mixed, so 55% indeterminate is unsurprising and the 135 classified cases are a non-random, more clear-cut subset

Overall survival and disease-free survival point in opposite directions by subtype (pancreatobiliary numerically longer OS but significantly shorter DFS), which is biologically incoherent and suggests differential post-recurrence treatment or informative censoring rather than a true subtype effect in either direction

Disease-free survival is positive for both regimens on adjusted Cox analysis (HR 0.69 and 0.68, both p = 0.02) while unadjusted DFS is flatly negative (p = 0.48), the same adjusted/unadjusted divergence as the primary endpoint - consistent with the adjustment carrying the result throughout

Delivery was poor: a fifth of the fluorouracil arm never received a dose, half of each chemotherapy arm did not complete six cycles, and median dose intensity was 78% and 88% of protocol. An intention-to-treat null result under that much non-receipt is uninformative about efficacy, and the authors do not report a per-protocol or dose-intensity sensitivity analysis
Screening data on how many patients were excluded and why were not collected routinely, so the degree of selection into the trial is unknown

Median survival of 35 months in the untreated observation arm is far better than the ampullary literature of the era, implying a fit, early-stage, highly selected population; the absolute benefit of adjuvant therapy in a frailer, node-positive clinic population cannot be read off this trial

Five patients randomised to gemcitabine were excluded post-randomisation as ineligible (3 metastatic, 2 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma) along with 1 in observation, a small departure from strict intention-to-treat that moves in the direction of the treatment arms
22782416.n: 434 randomised, 428 in the primary analysis (144 observation, 143 fluorouracil plus folinic acid, 141 gemcitabine); 297 ampullary, 96 intrapancreatic bile duct, 35 other (10 duodenal, 25 nondescript); 244 deaths (57%) at analysis
22782416.bottom_line: The only randomised trial of adjuvant chemotherapy in resected periampullary cancer was negative on its primary endpoint (HR 0.86, p = 0.25) and became positive only in a prespecified multivariable analysis adjusting for age, bile duct histology, grade and nodal status (HR 0.75, p = 0.03) that the authors themselves call hypothesis generating; it establishes neither a benefit specific to ampullary cancer - the ampullary subgroup was never powered or formally tested - nor that intestinal and pancreatobiliary subtypes respond differently, since only 135 of 297 ampullary tumours could be subtyped at all.

JPN part funded by the Liverpool NIHR Pancreas Biomedical Research Unit; MM part funded by the Oxford NIHR Biomedical Research Centre. Sponsors stated to have had no role in design, conduct, analysis or manuscript. No author conflicts of interest reported.

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that the ampullary-NOS category doubles as a waste-basket for cases that cannot be confidently assigned, and that whether the intra-ampullary group's survival advantage reflects small invasion size or a genuinely different biology is unknown
They acknowledge the periampullary-duodenal versus duodenal carcinoma survival comparison failed to reach significance because of small numbers
critique: The four categories were assigned retrospectively from archived gross descriptions and slides by the same authors who devised the scheme - no blinded or independent reassignment, and no interobserver agreement statistic, so the reproducibility of the gross algorithm that the whole classification rests on is untested here

The periampullary-duodenal group that anchors the favourable-prognosis claim has only 12 patients, 6 of them node positive; the survival estimates carry no confidence intervals anywhere in the paper and no multivariable model adjusting for T stage, node status or invasion size is reported despite a Cox model being described in the methods

Invasion size - the variable that drives the survival ordering - was in part estimated by applying an invasive/non-invasive ratio read off slides to the gross size, i.e. derived rather than measured, which biases exactly the comparison between the preinvasive-rich (intra-ampullary) and preinvasive-poor (ampullary-ductal) groups

Comparators are convenience cohorts from the same archives (113 PDAC, 55 duodenal) with no matching for stage, size, node status or treatment, and adjuvant therapy is not recorded at all, so the headline 'ampullary carcinoma is distinct from PDAC' survival gap conflates stage migration and resectability with biology

Follow-up was partly obtained from SEER and by telephoning treating physicians, with cases carrying missing values excluded variable by variable, so denominators shift between tables without being stated

Reclassifying 21% of cases out of the ampullary category inevitably removes the worst-prognosis tumours (mostly pancreatic) from the ampullary group, which mechanically improves ampullary survival relative to the historical literature - a definitional effect the paper presents as a biological finding
23026934.n: 249 strictly defined ampullary carcinomas culled from 1469 malignant pancreatoduodenectomy specimens, compared with 113 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas and 55 non-ampullary duodenal carcinomas
23026934.bottom_line: Establishes a reproducible-in-principle anatomic definition of ampullary carcinoma and shows that four gross/microscopic site-specific subsets differ markedly in stage and outcome, but the prognostic separation rests on small, unadjusted, single-reader subgroups and does not establish the classification's reproducibility or independence from stage.
23026934.funding: Supported in part by the Georgia Cancer Coalition Distinguished Cancer Clinicians and Scientists Program; authors declare no financial interest in any commercial company pertaining to the article

limitations: Retrospective design with no predefined criteria for proceeding from EUS to endoscopic or surgical resection, which may have produced inconsistent surgical referral and influenced endoscopic outcomes
The exact length of intraductal extension was not documented (only that it ranged from subcentimetre to about 1 cm)
The data represent only the subset of ampullary tumours at the institution that had EUS, since some patients went directly to ERCP
critique: The reference standard is circular for the lesions that matter most: for endoscopically resected adenomas, absence of intraductal extension was assumed whenever resection was complete with a negative margin and cholangiography showed no ductal extension - so EUS is being validated partly against a composite that already includes EUS-era endoscopic judgement, which inflates specificity and accuracy

The two comparisons use different denominators (90, 102 and 81 patients) drawn from the same cohort by availability of ERCP or of a resection specimen, so the claim that EUS and ERCP 'perform similarly' compares non-overlapping subsets rather than paired readings in the same patients

Sensitivity rests on very few events: 9-12 patients with intraductal extension in each analysis, which is why the AUROC confidence intervals are wide and why the EUS-versus-ERCP difference cannot be resolved

The 90% T-staging accuracy is carried almost entirely by correctly calling 65 of 66 lesions confined to the ampulla; for the invasive categories that would actually change management, accuracy was 78-80% and EUS systematically understaged

Six endosonographers and six ERCP endoscopists over 15 years, with no blinding, no central re-reading and no interobserver data; the authors concede EUS is operator dependent and that their results may reflect high-volume performance, which limits transfer to community practice

The 91% complete-resection rate is presented as evidence that EUS triaged patients well, but it is a before-after comparison with the same group's earlier 73% series and could equally reflect cohort selection, era effects or stricter criteria; patients deemed unresectable at EUS were excluded from that earlier study, making the two rates non-comparable

A 1998-2012 accrual spans radial and linear instruments and major changes in echoendoscope technology (GF-UM20 through GF-UC140P), and the radial/linear comparison is reported on 75 versus 21 patients without a formal test

The 17% non-adenomatous rate on papillectomy is a striking finding about referral biopsy reliability, but it also means the cohort's composition - and therefore every accuracy estimate - depends on outside histology that the centre did not verify
25293823.n: 119 patients undergoing EUS for an ampullary lesion (99 with adenoma or adenocarcinoma); ERCP in 90; surgical pathology available for 102 (EUS comparison) and 81 (ERCP comparison); 58 underwent endoscopic papillectomy
25293823.bottom_line: In expert hands and with no biliary stent in place, EUS stages ampullary lesions about as well as ERCP against surgical pathology and is excellent at confirming T1 disease, but it misses roughly a fifth of intraductal extensions and a fifth of deeper invasion, and this retrospective design with a partly circular reference standard cannot show that adding EUS improves resection outcomes.
25293823.funding: None stated; all authors disclosed no relevant financial relationships

limitations: No limitations section. The authors note that the retrospective series yielded fewer polyps with fewer biopsies and attribute between-centre variation in reported prevalence (28% to 100%) to the same technical differences

They state that upper gastrointestinal cancer develops slowly in FAP, with a median interval of 22 years after colectomy in a cited series of 37 patients, so natural history was not observed in this study

They acknowledge that the natural history of these polyps is largely unknown, which is why the mortality of prophylactic pancreatoduodenectomy must be weighed against it, and that endoscopic removal is often impractical while photodynamic therapy and vitamin C chemoprevention are unproven
critique: THE STAGING SYSTEM THAT THIS LITERATURE STILL USES WAS NEVER VALIDATED HERE. It was devised from a single cross-sectional screening round, with the four components and their cut-points assigned by the authors on the basis of 'known adenoma/cancer risk factors' rather than derived from or tested against any cancer outcome. No patient in this paper developed duodenal cancer during the study, so the association between stage IV and malignancy is asserted, not measured - and the four subsequent decades have never produced a formal validation, as the Mavani paper in this depot notes

The score has no weighting rationale: polyp number, size, histology and dysplasia each contribute 1-3 points as though equally important, and the stage boundaries (0, 1-4, 5-6, 7-8, 9-12) are arbitrary breaks in a 4-12 point range. Later work in this depot shows large polyp size rather than polyp number carries the cancer risk, and that the score omits the papilla entirely despite this very paper showing that is where the disease concentrates

The paper's own strongest finding - that the papilla is twice as likely to be adenomatous as the surrounding duodenum and that periampullary biopsy found adenoma in 11 patients with an otherwise normal duodenum - is not incorporated into the score that the paper proposes, an internal inconsistency that took until the 2019 ESGE guideline to correct

Because the score requires histology for two of its four components, it mandates biopsy of duodenal polyps and the papilla; ampullary biopsy is now known to cause pancreatitis and to produce fibrosis that compromises later endoscopic resection, so the system creates a harm that current guidelines explicitly try to avoid

47 of the 102 prospective patients also contribute to the retrospective series, so the prospective-versus-retrospective yield comparison is a within-patient comparison of two eras presented alongside a between-series comparison, and the 190-540% increases conflate better instruments, a single experienced endoscopist, and more biopsies without separating them

Everything is cross-sectional: 'stage IV occurred more often in the elderly' is a prevalence observation across ages, not progression, and cannot distinguish disease progression from cohort effects or ascertainment

No interobserver or intraobserver reproducibility data for polyp counting, size estimation or dysplasia grading, the four inputs to the score. Two of the ongoing studies the Soons review lists, three decades later, are still trying to establish exactly this

The mortality comparison used to motivate the programme (9 upper GI versus 4 rectal cancer deaths) comes from a separate 1948-1987 cohort of 197 patients with no denominators by follow-up time and no competing-risk accounting, in an era when colectomy practice and rectal surveillance differed entirely from the screened population

The bile-exposure hypothesis for the distal duodenal and periampullary distribution is offered with experimental and epidemiological citations but no measurement in these patients, and the search for a bile tumour promoter it launched has not succeeded

The surveillance intervals recommended (3 years for mild/moderate, at least yearly for stage IV) are stated without any analysis of interval cancers, cost or patient burden, and remain substantially the intervals in use today

The text extraction for this paper is incomplete and damaged: the 'Severity of duodenal polyposis' table - which carried the number of patients per stage and the mean polyp measurements - renders as an empty stub, and the file continues into an unrelated Lancet article on cell-surface peptidases, so the per-stage distribution beyond the 11 stage IV patients cannot be verified from this source
2571019.n: 102 patients screened prospectively (69 families, 59 men, 43 women, mean age 41 years, range 14-66); retrospective series 94 patients with 163 endoscopies (61 families, mean age at first endoscopy 39 years, range 15-73), of whom 47 overlapped with the prospective study
2571019.bottom_line: The paper that established that duodenal and periampullary adenomas are near-universal in FAP, concentrate on the papilla, and have displaced colorectal cancer as a cause of death - and that introduced the Spigelman stage still used to set surveillance intervals; but the score was constructed by expert judgement from a single cross-sectional screening round with no cancer outcomes, has never been formally validated, and conspicuously omits the ampulla that the same paper identified as the highest-risk site.
2571019.funding: ADS supported by the St Mark's Research Foundation; the Imperial Cancer Research Fund enabled purchase of the side-viewing video-endoscope for the St Mark's endoscopy unit

limitations: Retrospective and multi-institutional, so the gross dissection and node-sampling method was not standardised across centres
Data on adjuvant therapy were not available
Retrospective design can establish association only, not causation
critique: The missing adjuvant-therapy data are not a minor gap: node-positive patients are precisely the ones most likely to have received chemotherapy, so the N1/N2 hazard ratios are confounded by treatment in an unknown direction

The cut-points were not derived here - they were imported from Kang's SEER analysis - yet no attempt is made to test alternative thresholds (the paper's own Table 3 lists published cut-offs of 2, 3 and 4 nodes), so this is a single-threshold confirmation rather than a validation of the optimal threshold

Node yield varied from 1 to 61, and 52% of cases had fewer than 12 nodes; understaging in that half inflates the apparent N0 survival, which is the comparison that makes substaging look useful. The authors note the N0 and N1 curves overlap once sampling is adequate but still recommend the scheme, and the implication - that N1 may carry little prognostic weight over N0 when staging is done properly - is left unresolved rather than treated as a finding against the proposal

N2 cases were markedly over-represented at the one institution using the orange-peeling dissection method (26% vs 13.5% elsewhere), so the N1/N2 split is partly a marker of which pathology lab handled the specimen

Half the cohort was alive at analysis (155/308) with median follow-up only 56 months, so the 5-year estimates for N1 and N2 (31.5% and 30%, essentially identical) rest on few events and offer no separation at the time point clinicians use
No competing-risk analysis in a cohort with mean age 64 and median survival approaching 9 years in the N0 group, where non-cancer death is a substantial competing event

Interobserver agreement on the ampullary-origin determination by the five reviewers is not reported, although the same group showed elsewhere that related ampullary classifications are only fairly reproducible
25783680.n: 313 invasive ampullary carcinomas; 142 (45%) node positive; median 11 nodes examined (range 1-61); 150 (48%) had 12 or more nodes examined
25783680.bottom_line: Shows in a pathologically verified cohort that the number of metastatic nodes stratifies survival in ampullary carcinoma and supports adding an N1/N2 split to TNM, but the effect is modest, unadjusted for adjuvant therapy, and the N0-versus-N1 distinction largely disappears once at least 12 nodes are examined.
25783680.funding: None stated; authors declare no affiliation with or financial involvement in any organisation with a financial interest in the subject matter

limitations: Small sample size: this was explicitly a pilot study with no prospective power calculation, and an adequately powered study is needed to compare pancreatitis rates between the two methods
Risk factors for post-procedural pancreatitis were not investigated and may have confounded the results
The authors state they cannot conclude that recurrence was higher in the conventional group because that group included three patients with cancer whereas the wire-guided group had none
critique: A pilot study with no power calculation and 7 events across 45 patients cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction; reporting p = 0.960 for the primary endpoint without a confidence interval around the 5-point difference presents imprecision as equivalence

The one statistically significant clinical finding - 37.5% versus 0% pancreatitis with failed versus successful stenting inside the conventional arm - is a post-randomisation subgroup comparison between patients who differ precisely by whether the anatomy and bleeding allowed a stent, i.e. by procedural difficulty. It is quoted in later guidelines as supporting prophylactic stenting but is observational and confounded by the difficulty that caused the failure

The intervention is entangled with pancreatography: guidewire insertion deep into the duct prompted more pancreatograms (68% vs 42%) and longer guidewire dwell, which the authors propose as the reason the technique did not help. That makes the comparison one of two procedural packages, not of the wire technique in isolation

Randomisation was stratified by centre with seven operators across four hospitals and only 45 patients, so each operator contributed a handful of cases; no operator or centre effect is examined and the learning curve for a novel monorail technique is unaddressed
No blinding of operators or outcome assessors, and pancreatitis definitions were by consensus criteria but ascertainment depended on local practice at four centres

Three malignancies and two non-neoplastic lesions were resected despite exclusion criteria aiming to remove them, which means pre-procedure selection failed in 11% of cases and the two arms ended up with different disease mixes (3 malignant in conventional, 0 in wire-guided) - unbalancing both the recurrence and the resection-completeness comparisons

Complete resection was 91% versus 78% (p = 0.414), a 13-point difference that the paper treats as no difference; with 45 patients this analysis had essentially no power, so the technique's effect on the outcome that matters most is simply unknown

Follow-up was a median of about 13-14 months with a protocol of endoscopy at 1 week, 3, 6 and 12 months, far too short for the recurrence pattern described elsewhere in this depot (median time to recurrence 6 months but events out to nearly 10 years), so the zero recurrences in the wire-guided arm is uninformative

Severe bleeding requiring arterial embolisation occurred only in the wire-guided arm and perforation only in the wire-guided arm; with 1 event each these are uninterpretable, but they are not weighed against the stenting advantage in the conclusion
26479271.n: 48 patients referred, 45 randomised and analysed (22 wire-guided, 23 conventional); median age 56 years (range 32-76); procedures by seven expert endoscopists each performing more than 300 ERCPs per year with more than 30 prior papillectomies
26479271.bottom_line: Wire-guided papillectomy makes prophylactic pancreatic stenting almost always achievable (100% vs 65%) but did not reduce post-papillectomy pancreatitis (18% vs 13%) in this underpowered pilot; its most quoted finding - no pancreatitis when a stent went in versus 37.5% when it failed - is a post-randomisation comparison confounded by procedural difficulty.
26479271.funding: Not stated; all authors declare no conflicts of interest or financial ties

limitations: Retrospective nature of the study
Disparities in surveillance duration between patients
Some selection bias because some FAP patients do not undergo surveillance oesophagogastroduodenoscopy
Lack of biopsies of tiny lesions, particularly those under 10 mm, prevented pathological assessment of those lesions
The observation period was not sufficiently long to analyse the natural history of duodenal adenomatosis in FAP
Genetic testing for APC is not covered by Japanese national health insurance and was performed only in research settings, so genotype-phenotype correlations could not be examined
critique: The paper is quoted as validating the Spigelman classification, but 8 patients were stage IV and the entire validation rests on 4 or 5 high-grade dysplasia events among them. The two figures given (63% in the abstract and conclusions, 50% in the results and discussion) are never reconciled, so even the numerator of the headline result is uncertain

The outcome validated is high-grade dysplasia, not cancer. Only one invasive carcinoma occurred in the whole cohort and it was present at the first endoscopy, so the study observed essentially no incident duodenal cancer and cannot speak to cancer risk by stage - yet 'short-interval endoscopic surveillance and appropriate endoscopic resection may help prevent duodenal invasive carcinoma' is the stated conclusion

Spigelman stage is systematically underestimated by the study's own protocol: lesions under 10 mm were not biopsied, ampullary tumours under 10 mm were not biopsied at all, and patients without a biopsy were assigned the minimum dysplasia and histology score of 1 point each. Only 41 of 47 patients had any histology. Assigning floor values to unbiopsied patients shifts them towards stage 0-II and concentrates events in stage IV by construction - a circularity that inflates the apparent discrimination

The claim that no cancer occurred in stages I-III is uninterpretable when stage I had zero patients and the stage assignment for the stage 0 group (33 patients, 7 of whom later rose to stage II) was partly made by default scoring

The two stage IV patients who declined treatment and remained stable for 4-5 years are reported as reassuring, but 2 patients observed for 4 years in a disease with a reported 22-year interval to cancer carries no information about the safety of non-intervention

Treatment was not allocated by any rule: 9 patients had EMR 'because of their size, macroscopic type, or patient request' while 37 were observed, so the comparison between resected and observed patients is confounded by the same features that determine risk, and no analysis adjusts for it

Zero local relapse after EMR in 9 patients is presented as durability, but the companion literature in this depot reports recurrence after duodenal EMR in FAP of 22-100%; with 9 patients and 16 lesions this cohort had no power to detect that

Follow-up is heterogeneous by design (range 0-17 years, 1-40 endoscopies, some patients examined once) and no person-time denominators, cumulative incidence curves or confidence intervals appear anywhere, so every proportion in the paper is a crude count over an undefined observation period

The exclusion of the 4 ampulla-only patients and the protocol decision not to biopsy small ampullary tumours removes the highest-risk site in FAP from a study about duodenal cancer prevention - the opposite of the direction European guidelines took two years later - and 36% of the analysed patients had coexisting ampullary tumours that were never characterised

Selection into the cohort was through a national cancer centre where 84% had already had colectomy and 73% had a known family history, so this is a referred, surveillance-adherent population; the 66% duodenal neoplasia prevalence and the absence of deaths cannot be generalised to FAP patients who are not under specialist follow-up, as the authors partly concede

Histology was converted between Japanese and Western criteria, with Japanese non-invasive carcinoma recoded as high-grade dysplasia; the primary endpoint is therefore a translated category, and no agreement data between the two pathologists are given
The statement that no relationship was found between duodenal carcinoma incidence and surveillance interval is made with one carcinoma in the cohort
27306941.n: 77 FAP patients (50 men, 27 women, mean age at first endoscopy 40 +/- 14 years); duodenal neoplasia in 51 (66%); 47 analysed for non-ampullary duodenal lesions after excluding 4 whose neoplasms were confined to the ampulla; median observation period 8.5 years (range 0-17) for the whole cohort and 10.0 years (0-17) for those with duodenal lesions
27306941.bottom_line: In 77 Japanese FAP patients followed a median of 8.5 years with annual endoscopy and selective endoscopic resection, no one died of duodenal neoplasia and high-grade dysplasia arose only in Spigelman stage IV patients, which the authors read as supporting the classification; but the result rests on 4 or 5 events among 8 stage IV patients, only one invasive cancer occurred in the entire cohort, and unbiopsied small and ampullary lesions were scored at floor values - so stage assignment and outcome are not independent.
27306941.funding: Not stated; the authors declare they have nothing to disclose

limitations: The high frequency of pancreatobiliary-predominant cases raises the possibility of bias in the authors' criteria, and all five observers had an interest in pancreatobiliary pathology and may have been primed to read patterns as pancreatobiliary, although they were also exposed to lower GI pathology
Population differences between cohorts may account for the subtype frequencies differing from other series
The study was not controlled for patient treatment or management, though the authors state no known treatment bias was applied
Histologic typing on endoscopic or image-guided biopsies should be regarded as preliminary, and tissue-microarray-based immunohistochemical studies should be interpreted with caution or avoided
Larger cohorts with pathologic verification by multiple observers are needed to explain between-series differences in subtype frequency
critique: The one survival difference the paper reports as significant is an artefact of the analysis chosen: the biologically honest purist classification showed no survival difference at all (p = 0.65), and only after 94 indeterminate mixed tumours were force-assigned to a side did a difference appear - a reclassification that moves 40% of the cohort on the basis of a judgement with only moderate agreement

Even that difference was not independent of stage, budding or nodes, so the paper's own data argue against using subtype to select therapy, yet the abstract still describes the forced-binary classification as having 'good prognostic value'

'The study was not controlled for patient treatment' cannot be waved away with 'no known treatment bias': adjuvant regimens were already being chosen by subtype in this era, so the subtype-survival comparison may be measuring differential treatment

Kappa was computed across five observers over four or three unordered categories without reporting pairwise kappas or category-specific agreement, so it is not possible to see whether the failure is concentrated in the mixed/other categories or extends to the pure ones

Selecting for an invasive component greater than 3 mm removes exactly the small, mostly intra-ampullary tumours where subtyping is hardest and where the classification would most change management, so the reported 23-35% full agreement is an optimistic ceiling for routine practice and biopsies

The 476 PDAC comparator cohort is described as 'previously unpublished' from the authors' database with no inclusion criteria, dates, stage distribution or treatment given; the size- and node-matched HR of 1.97 rests on an undocumented control group

Pure intestinal carcinoma comprised only 13 cases, so every survival statement about the intestinal phenotype under the purist scheme is based on a group too small to interpret, and no confidence intervals are given for any median

Tumour budding is reported as an independent prognostic factor using criteria the same group published, with no reproducibility data of its own, so the variable that displaces subtype in the multivariable model is itself unvalidated here
27586202.n: 232 resected invasive ampullary carcinomas with an invasive component greater than 3.0 mm (from 249 strictly defined ampullary carcinomas among 1469 pancreatoduodenectomies); comparator cohort 476 pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas
27586202.bottom_line: This is the study that shows the intestinal-versus-pancreatobiliary classification is only fairly reproducible (kappa 0.39, full agreement in 23%), that 40% of ampullary carcinomas are morphologically mixed, and that any survival difference between subtypes appears only after forced binary assignment and is not independent of stage, budding or nodal status - so subtype should not by itself drive adjuvant decisions; it also confirms that even pancreatobiliary-type ampullary cancer behaves far better than pancreatic cancer.
27586202.funding: Not stated; authors declare no conflict of interest

limitations: The paper carries no limitations section; the authors frame the trial as pragmatic and present the result as establishing a new standard of care

They acknowledge that comparisons with CONKO-001 and JASPAC-1 are confounded by differing inclusion criteria, particularly CONKO-001's exclusion of postoperative CA19-9 above 92.5 KU/L, by differing rates of R1 resection (17% vs 60% between studies) and by differences in grade and nodal positivity

They note that numerous factors - distribution of adverse prognostic factors, dose intensity of per-protocol therapy, cumulative toxicity and fatigue, and ability to deliver second-line salvage therapy - should be considered when comparing across trials
critique: The trial was stopped and reported early on the DSMC's recommendation at 458 of 480 planned deaths with a p value of 0.032; early reporting on a nominally positive interim signal systematically overestimates effect size, and no alpha-spending adjustment for the early look is presented

A 2.5-month median gain with HR 0.82 (0.68-0.98) is a borderline result presented as a 'step change'; the 5-year survival figures (28.8% vs 16.3%) that carry the rhetorical weight come from the tail of curves with 43 months median follow-up, where few patients remain at risk and the confidence intervals overlap

Open-label design with no placebo means the control arm received no oral agent at all, so differential follow-up intensity, supportive care and second-line treatment are unblinded; post-recurrence therapy is not reported by arm

The benefit is confined to R0 patients in the margin-stratified analysis, with R1 medians of 23.7 versus 23.0 months - yet the abstract and the Research in Context box state that survival favoured the combination 'in most clinical subgroups, including patients with R1 resection margins', which the trial's own figure does not support

Nearly half the combination group (46%) discontinued before completing six cycles, so the regimen as delivered differs from the regimen as designed, and no dose-intensity or per-protocol analysis of the primary endpoint is reported beyond a statement that sensitivity analyses did not differ

Eight patients with stage IV tumours who 'were anxious to join the trial' were enrolled despite the protocol excluding distant metastasis, a protocol deviation that is reported without any sensitivity analysis excluding them

68 of 730 patients (9%) had postoperative CA19-9 imputed by multiple imputation, and CA19-9 is the strongest prognostic variable in the model that generates the adjusted HR of 0.79; the adjusted estimate therefore depends materially on imputed values in the covariate doing most of the work

This is pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with nonductal tumours explicitly excluded. Nothing in ESPAC-4 speaks to ampullary cancer, and its applicability to pancreatobiliary-subtype ampullary carcinoma - the usual justification offered - is an untested extrapolation across an entity whose resected median survival is roughly twice as long

The senior author reports grants, lecture fees and paid consultancy from numerous pharmaceutical companies including the manufacturers of relevant agents, in a trial whose practice-changing conclusion favours adding a proprietary oral agent; the funder itself (Cancer Research UK) is independent, but the comparator choice - gemcitabine monotherapy rather than fluorouracil plus folinic acid, which ESPAC-3 had shown to be equivalent - narrows the question in a way that favours a positive result
28129987.n: 732 randomised, 730 in the final analysis (366 gemcitabine, 364 gemcitabine plus capecitabine); reported after 458 of a target 480 deaths (95%); median follow-up 43.2 months
28129987.bottom_line: In resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, adjuvant gemcitabine plus capecitabine extended median overall survival by 2.5 months over gemcitabine alone (HR 0.82, p = 0.032) at no significant cost in overall toxicity, and became a standard of care - but the trial was reported early on a borderline signal, the benefit sits in R0 patients, and it says nothing directly about ampullary cancer, which was excluded.
28129987.funding: Cancer Research UK; the funder had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing. Extensive author financial relationships declared, including grants, lecture fees and paid consultancies from multiple pharmaceutical companies (declared as outside the submitted work).

limitations: Retrospective design with no predefined algorithm, relying on data not collected for the study
Unequal contribution of patients by each institution and a relatively small sample size
Reliance on histopathology of biopsies obtained before papillectomy without confirming the biopsy slides at the institution where papillectomy was performed

Given the retrospective design and the limited number of recurrences, no conclusion is possible about predictive parameters for recurrence (resection method, underlying histopathology, submucosal invasion)
critique: The paper's framing is the opposite of its own data: it is titled and presented as outcomes for benign ampullary lesions, yet 32% of the resected 'benign' lesions were adenocarcinoma. The 91% complete resection rate is therefore a mixed-histology figure, and the authors' own analysis shows margin positivity was confined to the cancers

Excluding 44.3% of papillectomies before analysis - those with malignant biopsy or suspicious appearance - is acknowledged as the reason for the low 6.8% surgical referral rate, but the same selection also removes the hardest resections, so the 91% completeness and 15.9% complication rates are not transferable to an unselected papillectomy practice

44 patients gives no power for any of the comparisons made: the high- versus low-volume complication comparison rests on 2 events in 6 procedures, and the single reported risk factor for incomplete resection comes from 4 incomplete resections

Recurrence is reported as 7 of 41 (17%) while the cohort is 44 - the denominator shift is unexplained - and median follow-up was 24 months with a floor of 6 months, so with a surveillance protocol stopping at annual intervals the figure is a minimum and cannot be compared with series reporting out to 5-10 years

6 of 7 recurrences were detected within 6 months, which by the definitions used in most of this literature would be residual rather than recurrent disease; conflating the two inflates 'recurrence' while hiding incomplete initial resection

The 24-study pooled table of 1121 patients against which this cohort is benchmarked is an informal narrative compilation with no systematic search, no quality assessment and no weighting - the stated 81.8% pooled success and 23.4% pooled complication rates should not be read as meta-analytic estimates

The claim that pre-papillectomy EUS was '100% accurate in ruling out greater than T1' rests on 16 patients in whom EUS reported T1N0 and none proved worse than T1 - a result with no discriminative information at all, since there were no positives to detect

EUS was done at the endoscopist's discretion and depended on institutional availability, so the EUS and no-EUS groups differ systematically; the fact that 3 of 3 patients with positive margins who were not operative candidates came from the no-EUS group is presented without acknowledging that comorbidity drove both decisions

Pancreatitis was 4.5%, lower than the 10.3% pooled figure, but the authors concede enzymes were measured only in patients with typical pain, so milder events were not ascertained - a point that applies equally to their favourable comparison with the literature
An 11-year accrual at the two large centres versus 2 years at the small ones means era and centre volume are completely confounded, yet the comparison between them is presented as informative
29755017.n: 44 of 79 patients (55.7%) who underwent endoscopic papillectomy for presumptively benign ampullary lesions; 38 procedures (86.3%) at high-volume and 6 (12.7%) at low-volume centres; 29 women and 15 men, median age 64 years (33-84); median follow-up 24 months (6-84)
29755017.bottom_line: Shows that endoscopic papillectomy achieves complete resection in about 90% with modest morbidity and no mortality in expert hands, and - more importantly - that even after excluding lesions that looked or biopsied malignant, a third of the specimens contained adenocarcinoma; but with 44 patients, a 24-month median follow-up and 44% of papillectomies excluded, it cannot define recurrence risk or its predictors.
29755017.funding: The authors declared that this study received no financial support

limitations: The authors note that the overall survival data remain immature, with the trial ongoing at 3 years of follow-up at publication
Disease-free survival is not validated as a surrogate endpoint for overall survival in adjuvant pancreatic cancer trials, although in this trial it was robust and correlated with overall survival

The median overall survival in the gemcitabine group (35.0 months) was longer than in previous phase 3 adjuvant trials (20.1-26.5 months), which the authors attribute to the high use of FOLFIRINOX after relapse in 76% of those patients
critique: Eligibility was unusually restrictive even for an adjuvant trial: WHO performance status 0-1 only, age under 80, CA19-9 under 180 U/mL, full recovery from surgery and no symptomatic cardiac disease. Patients who are frail, jaundiced, slow to recover or have a high CA19-9 - a large part of any real postoperative clinic - were excluded, so the 54-month median survival is not a population estimate and the absolute benefit will be smaller outside the trial

The trial was analysed and published early on the DSMC's recommendation, and the authors concede the survival data are immature; a median overall survival whose upper confidence limit is 'not reached' is an unstable estimate on which to base the 19.4-month claim

Crossover was effectively universal and asymmetric - 76% of relapsing gemcitabine patients received FOLFIRINOX afterwards - which the authors invoke to explain the unusually good control-arm survival; this means the trial measures the value of giving the combination first rather than later, a narrower question than the headline implies

The regimen changed mid-trial: irinotecan was reduced from 180 to 150 mg/m2 after 162 patients and 24 patients received intermediate doses, so three dose levels are pooled into one arm; the subgroup comparison reassuring on efficacy had wide confidence intervals (0.67-1.40)

Three-quarters of the experimental arm had grade 3 or 4 toxicity and 21 patients stopped for adverse events, yet no patient-reported quality-of-life outcome is reported in the primary publication, so the trade-off a patient faces cannot be quantified

In the fifth of patients aged 70 or over - closer to the median age of ampullary and periampullary cancer - the primary endpoint benefit vanished (HR 0.86, 0.53-1.39). This is reported as a subgroup without an interaction test, but it is the subgroup most relevant to the older populations in whom the regimen is now often considered
Two patients in the FOLFIRINOX arm were found to have metastatic disease at enrolment and were 'included in error', with no sensitivity analysis excluding them

The primary endpoint is disease-free survival in an open-label trial where imaging follow-up was by protocol but unblinded; the authors concede DFS is not a validated surrogate in this disease, and relying on it in an unblinded trial admits ascertainment bias in the direction of the arm expected to do better

This trial excluded nonductal pancreatic tumours by design. Applying its result to ampullary adenocarcinoma - whether pancreatobiliary or intestinal subtype - has no support in the trial and would transplant a 75.9% grade 3-4 toxicity regimen into a disease with roughly double the baseline resected survival and no randomised evidence that any adjuvant chemotherapy helps

The trial received a grant from Chugai Pharmaceutical via R&D Unicancer and most senior authors report fees from pharmaceutical companies; the comparator was gemcitabine monotherapy rather than the gemcitabine plus capecitabine that ESPAC-4 had reported as superior the previous year, so by the time of publication the control arm was already not the best available standard
30575490.n: 493 patients randomised (247 modified FOLFIRINOX, 246 gemcitabine; safety population 238 and 243); median follow-up 33.6 months (95% CI 30.3-36.0)
30575490.bottom_line: In a fit, highly selected population with resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, adjuvant modified FOLFIRINOX roughly doubled median disease-free survival (21.6 vs 12.8 months) and added 19 months of median overall survival over gemcitabine at the cost of grade 3-4 toxicity in three-quarters of patients, with no demonstrable benefit in patients aged 70 or over; it provides no evidence for ampullary cancer, which was excluded.
30575490.funding: R&D Unicancer (which received a grant from Chugai Pharmaceutical), a Clinical Research Hospital Program grant (PHRC11-006) from the French Ministry of Health and the Institut National du Cancer, the French National League against Cancer; the Canadian arm by a Program Grant (704970) from the Canadian Cancer Society and grants from 7 Days in May. Extensive author disclosures of consulting, advisory and travel support from industry.

limitations: Retrospective and nonrandomised, so the associations cannot be interpreted as causal
Regression modelling and propensity-score matching adjust for unbalanced measured covariates but remain vulnerable to unmeasured confounders
Treatment completion and treatment-related toxicity were not captured, although they matter for the decision to use adjuvant therapy

Disease rarity may have limited power for some analyses; in particular the 2-by-2 substratification of agent against subtype was probably underpowered and the multiagent subgroup analyses were limited because gemcitabine monotherapy was the most common regimen, although there were no trends in any such comparison
The findings do not apply to neoadjuvant therapy, which was not used in this series
The authors note that exclusion of patients who died within 90 days was deliberately done to minimise immortal time bias
critique: 369 of 756 patients (49%) were excluded for unknown histologic subtype - a larger group than the one analysed. Since subtype is recorded more often when a specialist pathologist reviewed the case or when the tumour was morphologically unambiguous, the analysed cohort is systematically the clearer, probably more specialist-managed half, and the paper gives no comparison of excluded versus included patients

Subtype was determined by institutional pathology review across 12 centres with no central re-review and no immunohistochemistry, justified by a 2004 paper on cytokeratin/histology correlation. Given that blinded multi-observer studies put morphological subtyping at kappa 0.39 with 40% of tumours mixed, substantial misclassification is certain, and misclassification would bias any subtype-by-agent interaction towards null - exactly the result reported

Propensity matching discarded 195 of 357 patients and then used only 81 pairs, which gives the central negative result wide confidence intervals (intestinal 0.67-2.16, pancreatobiliary 0.66-2.76). These intervals do not exclude a clinically important benefit of 25-35% relative risk reduction, so 'no benefit' is better stated as 'no benefit detectable with this power'

The agent-by-subtype cells are tiny: 31 pancreatobiliary and 34 intestinal patients had a classifiable regimen, and the Kaplan-Meier risk tables show as few as 9 patients in the pancreatobiliary fluorouracil arm. The paper's own concession that this 2-by-2 matrix was underpowered should be read as meaning the primary hypothesis was not actually testable in this dataset

Matching was on age, race/ethnicity, pT, nodal status and perineural invasion but not on grade, lymphovascular invasion, margin status, CA19-9 or year of surgery, despite grade, LVI and margin all differing between the treated and untreated groups on univariate analysis; residual confounding by indication therefore persists in the matched cohort and runs against adjuvant therapy

Excluding deaths within 90 days protects against immortal time bias in one direction but introduces survivor selection in the other, since patients fit enough to survive 90 days and then start chemotherapy are being compared with patients who survived 90 days without it; a time-varying or landmark analysis at the actual start of chemotherapy is not performed

Race appears as one of the strongest predictors of death (Black race HR 3.93) and of treatment omission (OR 0.26), which signals unmeasured access, comorbidity and socioeconomic confounding that no propensity model built on tumour variables can absorb - and which the paper does not discuss

Median follow-up in the matched cohort is only 34 months against a median survival of 57 months, so more than half the survival curve is driven by censoring; 5-year actuarial estimates from such immature data are unstable

A 17-year accrual spans the introduction of modern multiagent regimens; gemcitabine monotherapy predominated, so the trial tests the agents of the 2000s and cannot speak to FOLFIRINOX-era therapy - a point the authors make for multiagent therapy but not for the headline conclusion

In the multivariable Cox table most hazard ratios are reported as 'NA' with only a p value, including the adjuvant therapy row, so the magnitude and precision of the central negative finding in the unmatched analysis cannot be inspected

The pancreatic fistula analysis compares this cohort against an entirely separate Pancreas Fistula Study Group dataset of 4722 non-ampullary resections with no matching for era, centre or surgeon, so the 2.7-fold fistula odds are a cross-dataset comparison rather than a within-cohort finding
31141112.n: 357 patients from 756 resections after serial exclusion (196 intestinal, 138 pancreatobiliary, 16 mixed, 7 other); 200 (56.0%) received adjuvant therapy; propensity-matched cohort 162 (81 surgery alone, 81 adjuvant therapy)
31141112.bottom_line: The largest multi-institutional series with complete histologic and adjuvant-therapy detail found no survival benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, or subtype-matched regimens after resection of ampullary adenocarcinoma, with adjuvant therapy instead being given selectively to node-positive, perineural-invasion-positive disease; but half the screened patients were excluded for unknown subtype, subtype was assigned locally without central review, and only 81 matched pairs underpin the null result, so this excludes a large benefit rather than a modest one.
31141112.funding: None stated; conflict of interest disclosures reported as none

limitations: The guideline grades almost every duodenal and ampullary recommendation as low quality evidence, including all those that are nonetheless issued as strong recommendations
It states explicitly that there is a lack of data and a need to better understand the biology of duodenal and ampullary adenomas in order to develop a new risk-stratification system

It notes that obtaining all components of the Spigelman score requires pathology, which conflicts with its own recommendation against routine biopsy, and resolves this by allowing the stage to be determined from previous pathology or optical diagnosis
It acknowledges that long-term data on cancer risk in MAP patients with apparently less severe disease are hardly available, yet surveillance intervals follow the FAP recommendations
critique: The central new recommendation - separate ampullary intervals of 5, 3 and 1 year - carries no citation, no modelling and no stated derivation. The text says these intervals 'seem safe' and are 'proposed'; the only supporting evidence offered is that half of duodenal cancers are periampullary and that an abnormal ampulla predicted high-grade dysplasia in one study. A size threshold of 10 mm and three interval lengths have been generated by panel judgement and are now embedded in practice

Strong recommendations are repeatedly issued on low-quality evidence (duodenal surveillance from age 25, thorough ampullary inspection at every endoscopy, MAP surveillance from 35), which GRADE permits only under specific conditions that are not articulated here; the accompanying agreement percentages (89-100%) measure panel consensus, not evidence, and risk being read as a quality metric

The guideline keeps the Spigelman score as the primary determinant of interval while simultaneously discouraging the biopsies that generate two of its four components, and resolves the contradiction by permitting stage to be calculated from historical pathology or optical diagnosis. That makes the score a different quantity from the one described in 1989, and no accuracy data for optically assigned histology or dysplasia are provided

Recommending against routine ampullary biopsy on the basis of pancreatitis risk is reasonable but the cited evidence is four case reports and asymptomatic amylase elevation in a 35-patient study; the trade-off against losing histological risk stratification at the highest-risk site in FAP is not analysed

The guideline's own evidence summary shows recurrence after duodenal endoscopic resection of 22-100% across nine studies of 6-35 patients, one cited study showing that downstaging stage IV disease was followed by faster subsequent progression, and no demonstration that endoscopic therapy prevents cancer - yet it still suggests considering EMR for adenomas 10 mm or larger. The recommendation outruns the evidence the guideline itself presents

Interval recommendations diverge sharply from the American College of Gastroenterology for the same stage (3-6 months with surgical evaluation for stage IV versus 6 months here), and the guideline neither reconciles this nor explains the basis for the difference, leaving clinicians to choose between guidelines rather than between evidence

The cancer-risk figures that justify the whole programme (4-10% cumulative duodenal cancer risk by 60) are drawn from cohorts spanning decades in which endoscopic technology and Spigelman scoring both changed, a confounder the companion review in this depot flags explicitly but this guideline does not

The ampullary recommendation in the summary table - 'consider discussing endoscopic treatment in a multidisciplinary setting for adenomas 10 mm or larger, showing excessive growth, or with suspicion of invasive growth' - is a recommendation to hold a discussion rather than a decision rule, and gives no guidance on what the discussion should conclude

Interobserver reproducibility of the two optical judgements the guideline now relies on - ampullary appearance and polyp size - is never addressed, although ongoing trials of exactly this variability were registered at the time

No funding statement appears, and several panel members declare equipment loans, research donations, consultancies and speaker fees from endoscope manufacturers (Fujifilm, Olympus, Pentax, Cook Medical, Boston Scientific, Medtronic) in a guideline that intensifies endoscopic surveillance and recommends cap-assisted and side-viewing endoscopy; two panel members are co-editors of the publishing journal
31342472.bottom_line: The guideline that first separated ampullary from Spigelman-based surveillance in polyposis syndromes - 5, 3 or 1 year by ampullary appearance and size, with the shorter interval taking precedence, and biopsy discouraged - which is a sensible correction to a score that ignores where half the cancers arise; but the ampullary intervals are uncited panel judgement, every relevant recommendation rests on low-quality evidence, and the guideline recommends endoscopic resection despite its own summary showing 22-100% recurrence and no cancer-prevention data.

limitations: Retrospective design, defended on the grounds that no randomised trial in ampullary cancer exists and that well-defined multicentre cohorts from prospective databases are currently the best available option
Adjuvant regimens were heterogeneous, with no clear recommendations available for patient selection or agents, and this heterogeneity limits interpretation of the results
Newer multi-agent regimens such as FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel could not be evaluated
The subgroup of patients receiving fluorouracil-based combinations was too small to assess that regimen in the intestinal subtype
critique: The decisive confounder is stated plainly in the paper and then not handled: at the participating centres the decision to give adjuvant therapy was based on T3/4 stage, node positivity and raised CA19-9 after multidisciplinary discussion. Treatment was therefore allocated by prognosis, and no propensity matching, inverse-probability weighting or landmark analysis was performed anywhere in the study

That confounding by indication is visible in the whole-cohort result, where crude survival was 55 months LONGER without adjuvant therapy (168 vs 113 months, p = 0.608). A protective HR of 0.351 appearing only after the cohort is cut by subtype, from a dataset whose unstratified signal runs the other way, is the pattern of a subgroup artefact rather than of a real interaction

Several reported statistics are internally inconsistent, which undermines the central estimate: the whole-cohort multivariable ASA HR is 1.784 with CI 0.997-3.193 yet p = 0.050, N stage HR 1.831 with CI 0.904-3.707 yet p = 0.033, and in the subgroup the univariate adjuvant HR is given as 0.301 with CI 0.211-0.715 and T stage as 3.189 with CI 1.223-4.363 - point estimates lying outside or implausibly placed within their own confidence limits. A reader cannot take the 0.351 (0.151-0.851) at face value when neighbouring rows in the same table are arithmetically impossible

A median overall survival of 136.5 months (over 11 years) for resected ampullary cancer is far outside every other series in this literature (Ecker 57 months, Balci 56 months, ESPAC-3 ampullary 53 months). With median follow-up 80 months and medians exceeding it, these are extrapolations from heavily censored curves, and the whole survival scale of the paper is suspect - possibly reflecting loss to follow-up being treated as survival

No interaction test between subtype and adjuvant therapy is reported. Comparing a significant p value in one subgroup with a non-significant one in the other is not evidence of effect modification, and the intestinal subgroup had only 22 treated patients - a point estimate of HR 0.443 that is numerically in the same direction as the pancreatobiliary result but simply imprecise (CI 0.099-1.984)

Subtype was assigned locally at five centres across 21 years using the Albores-Saavedra criteria with no central review, no immunohistochemistry and no interobserver data. Mixed tumours (16 cases) were pooled with pancreatobiliary on the strength of two cited papers, a decision taken after seeing the data and one that directly shapes the subgroup in which the effect is claimed

A cohort assembled from 1996 to 2017 straddles the introduction of adjuvant gemcitabine itself, so untreated patients are enriched for the earlier era while treated patients are concentrated later; no adjustment for year of surgery appears in any model, and era is confounded with both treatment and supportive care

20% of treated patients had an unknown regimen and treatment completion, dose intensity and toxicity were not captured at all, so the exposure variable is 'any adjuvant therapy ever started' rather than a defined treatment

Only 35% of the cohort received adjuvant therapy, giving 53 treated pancreatobiliary/mixed patients to support a multivariable model that also contains ASA, CEA, T, N, grade and margin - far too few events per variable, which is the standard route to inflated hazard ratios

The in vitro observation that gemcitabine was active only in pancreatobiliary-type ampullary cell lines is offered as mechanistic support, but it comes from a paper co-authored by this group and cannot corroborate a clinical subgroup finding
Follow-up and recurrence surveillance protocols are not described, so differential detection between treated (closely followed) and untreated patients cannot be excluded
31987649.n: 214 patients undergoing pancreatoduodenectomy for ampullary cancer; 74 (34.6%) intestinal, 124 (57.9%) pancreatobiliary, 16 (7.5%) mixed (analysed as 140 pancreatobiliary/mixed); 75 (35.1%) received adjuvant therapy; median follow-up 80 months
31987649.bottom_line: Reports that gemcitabine-based adjuvant therapy is associated with longer survival in pancreatobiliary/mixed but not intestinal ampullary cancer, and proposes stratifying adjuvant treatment by subtype; but adjuvant therapy was allocated by prognostic stage at the treating centres with no attempt at adjustment for that selection, the whole-cohort effect runs the opposite way, no interaction was tested, and several of the reported hazard ratios are inconsistent with their own confidence intervals - so this is a hypothesis, not evidence for subtype-directed therapy.
31987649.funding: No funding was received for the design of the study, collection, analysis and interpretation of data, or writing of the manuscript; all authors declare no conflict of interest

limitations: The guideline grades 9 of its 11 main recommendations as low quality evidence, with only 3 statements (endoscopic papillectomy for adenoma without intraductal extension, direct snare resection without submucosal injection, and prophylactic pancreatic stenting) reaching moderate quality
It states that the literature search prioritised meta-analyses and prospective studies but that retrospective analyses and pilot studies had to be included where prospective data did not exist
It notes the 8th edition T subcategories are insufficiently precise, with no significant recurrence-free survival difference between T1b and T2 or between T2 and T3a
It acknowledges that the EUS-guided versus ERCP-guided drainage meta-analyses rest on small series from high-volume expert centres and are difficult to generalise
No additional high-quality evidence on preoperative and palliative biliary drainage had appeared since the 2017 ESGE stenting guideline
critique: Nine of eleven main recommendations are strong on low-quality evidence. The most consequential of these - pancreatoduodenectomy for any T1 or greater adenocarcinoma, including when found incidentally after papillectomy - is a major operation mandated on low-quality evidence, and the Korean propensity-matched study in this depot (Yoon 2023) subsequently found no overall survival difference between surveillance and completion surgery in exactly that situation

The size threshold for en bloc resection is given as '20-30 mm' in the recommendation but discussed elsewhere as 30 mm and as 4 cm for surgical referral, with intraductal involvement thresholds of 10 mm (resectable), 20 mm (surgery suggested) and 20 mm with ablation (possibly acceptable) appearing in different places. The practical cut-points a clinician needs are not stated consistently

The recommendation against routine molecular and immunohistochemical testing of ampullary biopsies was already at odds with the pathology literature when issued and is now clearly superseded: the PERIPAN consensus in this depot recommends reflex mismatch repair testing on every ampullary carcinoma, and the medullary-carcinoma data show 64% MMR deficiency with near-universal PD-L1 expression. A weak recommendation on low-quality evidence has nonetheless had the effect of discouraging testing that identifies Lynch syndrome and immunotherapy candidates

Prophylactic pancreatic stenting is graded moderate quality, but the randomised evidence in this depot amounts to Harewood's 19-patient trial that lost significance on intention-to-treat and Lee's 45-patient pilot in which guaranteed stenting did not reduce pancreatitis (18% vs 13%); grading that body of evidence as moderate overstates it

'Direct snare resection without submucosal injection' is also graded moderate quality and issued as a strong recommendation, yet the ESAP analysis published four years later notes the evidence remains contradictory and that submucosal injection was still used in a quarter of recent European papillectomies - an indication the panel's confidence exceeded the literature

The follow-up schedule - duodenoscopy with scar biopsies at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly for at least 5 years - is specified to the month on low-quality evidence with no derivation, no interval-cancer analysis and no cost or burden assessment. Subsequent data in this depot show recurrences out to 9.75 years, so 5 years may be too short, while the 3-month examination largely detects residual rather than recurrent disease

There is no recommendation on what to do with an Rx or indeterminate margin, which the Japanese national cohort later showed accounts for a quarter of papillectomies and carries almost the same recurrence risk as frank R1 - a gap that leaves the commonest ambiguous pathology result unaddressed

The guideline recommends against papillectomy when adenoma has not been proven, but the literature it reviews shows pre-procedure biopsy is wrong in 20-47% of cases in both directions; requiring proof of adenoma from a test that unreliable, while discouraging the biopsy repetition that might establish it, sets a standard that cannot be met in practice

Nothing in the guideline addresses the histologic subtype question or adjuvant therapy, so a clinician whose papillectomy specimen shows pancreatobiliary-subtype T1 adenocarcinoma is directed to pancreatoduodenectomy with no guidance on what, if anything, should follow

No funding statement appears. Four panel members including the lead author and the guideline committee chair declare consultancies, lecture fees or departmental research grants from Boston Scientific, Cook Medical, Olympus and Medtronic, in a guideline recommending specific endoscopic devices, stents and techniques

The panel is composed almost entirely of endoscopists; the surgical and pathological recommendations (pancreatoduodenectomy for T1, frozen-section policy during ampullectomy, what constitutes adequate histopathology) are made without evident surgical or pathology representation among the listed authors
33728632.bottom_line: The reference guideline for ampullary tumours: endoscopic papillectomy first-line for adenoma without intraductal extension, en bloc up to 20-30 mm without submucosal injection, prophylactic pancreatic stenting, surgery for intraductal extension over 20 mm or size over 4 cm, pancreatoduodenectomy for T1 or above including incidental post-papillectomy T1, and duodenoscopy with scar biopsies at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly for 5 years; but nine of eleven main recommendations are strong on low-quality evidence, its advice against molecular testing has since been reversed by the pathology consensus, and it gives no guidance on indeterminate margins.

limitations: The authors state that long-term efficacy and safety data for endoscopic therapy in the duodenum and at the ampullary site are almost entirely absent, that 6 of the 7 studies published in the preceding decade were single-centre retrospective series with at most 49 subjects, and that the absence of prospective international data makes the true effect of endoscopic therapy on prevention of duodenal surgery, cancer development and survival impossible to determine
No comparative studies exist between endoscopic therapy and surveillance with or without prophylactic surgery, nor between different endoscopic and surgical therapies
Guidelines on management of duodenal adenomas in adenomatous polyposis are mainly based on expert opinion because studies on clinical management are scarce
Long-term data on cancer risk in MAP patients with apparently less severe disease are hardly available, yet surveillance intervals follow the FAP recommendations
The authors explicitly suggest that given the absence of evidence on long-term efficacy, it may be time to reconsider the use of endoscopic therapy in FAP patients
critique: This is a narrative review presented with the trappings of a systematic one - a PubMed search string, a screened count of 2277 and an included count of 137 - but there is no second reviewer, no inclusion/exclusion protocol, no PRISMA flow, no risk-of-bias appraisal and no quantitative synthesis. The reader cannot tell why 137 of 2277 were kept or whether contrary evidence was excluded
