The 10-year search window excludes the foundational literature by design, including Spigelman's original paper, Groves' prospective duodenal cancer study and Bulow's cohort, all of which are nonetheless cited and relied upon - so the search strategy does not match the evidence base actually used

Ranges are reported without weighting by study size or quality, so '78-100% residual or recurrent disease' and '0-20% delayed bleeding' lump series of 6 patients with series of 49; no pooled estimate or heterogeneity assessment is attempted, which makes the numbers unusable for counselling a specific patient

The single illustrative patient does heavy rhetorical work. A man whose Spigelman stage fell from IV to III without intervention, who cancelled appointments repeatedly and who postponed his EMR is used to argue that 'it may well be time to reconsider the use of endoscopic therapy' - a conclusion drawn from one non-adherent patient and a literature of 181 patients total

The review's own recommendation to refer all ampullary adenomas of any size to an expert centre sits uneasily with its evidence that endoscopic ampullectomy in FAP recurs in 19-58% with pancreatitis in up to 30%, and no analysis addresses whether intervening on small ampullary adenomas does net good

Discouraging routine biopsy while retaining the Spigelman score creates an unresolved circularity the review acknowledges but does not solve: two of the four score components require histology, so under the modified approach the stage is calculated from historical pathology reports or optical diagnosis, which means the score is no longer the measured quantity it was validated (such as it was) against

The pancreatitis risk used to justify avoiding ampullary biopsy rests on 4 case reports plus asymptomatic amylase elevation in 30% of available tests in 35 patients - a weak evidence base for a practice change that removes histology from risk stratification

No quantitative comparison of the four guidelines' intervals against outcomes is attempted; the table shows ACG is substantially more intensive than ESGE for the same stage, and the review offers no basis for choosing between them other than noting the difference

The claim that surveillance improves life expectancy by 7 months comes from a 1997 decision analysis with modelled inputs, cited without any sensitivity analysis or discussion of how the modelled assumptions compare with current endoscopic practice

Cumulative incidence figures are repeated from primary sources without noting that the authors themselves caution that rising Spigelman scores over decades partly reflect technology - a caveat applied to stage IV prevalence but not to the 18% duodenal cancer risk at 75 that drives the whole surveillance rationale

The three ongoing studies cited as future prospects (NCT03346980 on inter- and intra-observer variability of Spigelman variables, NL8757 on inter-laboratory histopathology variability, NCT03847636 on cryoballoon ablation) are an admission that the reproducibility of the staging system has still not been established 30 years after its introduction - a point the review states but does not carry through to its recommendations
34529357.bottom_line: A useful, candid narrative synthesis showing that about half of FAP duodenal cancers are (peri)ampullary, that the Spigelman score does not capture ampullary risk and that ESGE and BSG have now added separate ampullary intervals; its most important message is negative - across only 181 patients in 7 small retrospective series there is no evidence that endoscopic therapy prevents duodenal cancer, delays surgery or improves survival - but it is a narrative review without protocol, appraisal or pooling, and its call to reconsider endoscopic therapy is anchored to a single non-adherent patient.
34529357.funding: None stated; the authors declare that there is no conflict of interest. No datasets were generated or analysed.

limitations: No limitations section. The authors note that the high dMMR yield in their duodenal cohort could be explained by preselection on young age, which enriches for hereditary predisposition
They acknowledge that large studies on duodenal carcinoma are either missing or include duodenal cases within mixed periampullary or small bowel cohorts
They state that false-negative immunohistochemistry can occur when an antigenically intact but catalytically inactive protein is present, which would show MSI but not protein loss
Because patient data were anonymised before collection, the results of germline analyses could not be shared with patients, their families or physicians
critique: THE AMPULLARY FINDING IS A NEGATIVE ONE BUILT ON A SINGLE CASE. Only 1 of 23 early-onset ampullary carcinomas was dMMR. The abstract's claim that 'all dMMR AC and PC were due to LS' and the conclusion that concordance 'warrants ubiquitous dMMR testing in all early-onset DC, AC, and PC' rest on 1 ampullary and 2 pancreatic patients; 1 of 1 and 2 of 2 are not estimates of concordance, and no confidence intervals appear anywhere in the paper

The recommendation for universal testing in ampullary cancer is therefore not supported by this dataset. Testing 23 patients to find 1 dMMR case yields a 4.3% prevalence indistinguishable from pancreatic cancer and lower than the roughly 10% the authors themselves cite for unselected ampullary carcinoma - which would mean selecting by young age performs worse than testing everyone, the opposite of the paper's framing. The companion paper in this depot (Xue 2023) found 15% dMMR in unselected non-medullary ampullary carcinoma

72 of 162 eligible patients (44%) were not included because their laboratories did not supply material, and no comparison of included with excluded patients on age, site, stage or centre is offered. In a nationwide registry study, non-random availability of archived blocks from 23 of an unstated number of laboratories is a serious selection problem for a prevalence estimate

Resection specimens only. Early-onset duodenal, ampullary and pancreatic cancers that were unresectable - the majority for pancreatic cancer - are absent by design, so the cohort is skewed towards earlier-stage, fitter patients and the prevalence figures cannot be read as population estimates for the cancers as diagnosed

A substantial number of registry-coded pancreatic cancers turned out to be ampullary on review, which is reported as a reclassification but never quantified against the original coding, and the review was by a single pathologist with no second reader or interobserver data. Since the whole point of the ampullary group is that it differs from pancreas, the reliability of the reassignment is central and untested

'Unclassified' is doing real work in the headline: 2 of 14 dMMR cases could not have germline testing because of material limitations, so the statement that dMMR indicates a hereditary defect is based on 10 of 12 assessable cases, and 2 of the Lynch assignments could not be confirmed by a second somatic hit because tumour sequencing failed (patients DC19 and PC13) or tumour cell percentage was too low (PC46)

The late-onset comparator is an internal Radboud cohort of 18 duodenal carcinomas with no stated selection criteria, no date range and a median age 27 years higher; it is a convenience group, and the p = 0.005 for early- versus late-onset dMMR rests on 1 event in that arm

No survival or treatment data are reported, so the clinical consequences the discussion invokes - better prognosis of dMMR tumours and eligibility for pembrolizumab - are imported from colorectal and small bowel literature rather than demonstrated here

Anonymisation before collection meant germline results could not be returned to patients or families. Identifying 8 Lynch and 2 CMMRD patients, whose relatives carry actionable risk, and being structurally unable to tell anyone is an ethical cost of the design that the paper records in a single sentence without discussion

The two CMMRD cases are presented as an additional incentive to test duodenal cancer, but both were already clinically obvious by their teens from multiple childhood malignancies and polyps; universal tumour testing is not what would identify such patients

dMMR tumours were larger across the whole series (p = 0.031) but not within any site, and the paper reports this as a finding without noting that an overall association driven by the duodenal group - which had both the largest tumours and nearly all the dMMR cases - is confounded by site
MSI was assessed by five mononucleotide markers or by a 55-marker NGS panel depending on tumour cellularity, two methods with different thresholds pooled into one 'MSI' variable
34873870.n: 90 early-onset carcinomas of 162 identified patients: 23 duodenal, 23 ampullary and 44 pancreatic, all under age 50 (median 43, range 17-49); comparator 18 late-onset (age 50 or over) duodenal carcinomas (median 70, range 57-77)
34873870.bottom_line: In a nationwide Dutch series of resected carcinomas diagnosed before age 50, mismatch repair deficiency was common in duodenal cancer (47.8%) and more than half of those cases were Lynch or CMMRD, so dMMR testing is clearly justified there; but only 1 of 23 early-onset ampullary and 2 of 44 pancreatic carcinomas were deficient, and the paper's recommendation to test all early-onset ampullary cancers rests on that single case - routine MMR testing in ampullary carcinoma is better justified by the unselected prevalence reported elsewhere than by age-based selection.
34873870.funding: A grant from the Dutch Cancer Society (KWF Kankerbestrijding) 2016 10289; no conflicts of interest were declared. Approved by the Radboud University Medical Center ethics committee (CMO-2017-3780) with PALGA Privacy Commission and Scientific Council approval.

limitations: Selection bias could not be avoided because indications for endoscopic papillectomy are not established
No guidelines exist on optimal technique, so many intra-procedural decisions were at the endoscopist's discretion
Not all hospitals distinguished margin positivity as vertical or lateral, so margins had to be simplified to positive/uncertain versus negative
Retrospective design meant procedural and follow-up factors could not be controlled
critique: The paper is internally inconsistent on its own numbers: the abstract states 11 patients (16.1%) had early recurrence and 13 (10.4%) late recurrence, while the results and tables give early 11 (10.4%) and late 13 (12.3%); the article-highlights section gives re-recurrence as 6 patients (12.3%) against 5.7% elsewhere. A reader cannot tell which denominators were used

The early/late recurrence split is the paper's novelty but it is defined by the timing of the first surveillance endoscopy, which was itself at the endoscopist's discretion within 3 months - so a patient's classification depends on when they happened to be scoped, not on biology, and the authors concede that delayed detection of a remnant leads to underestimating residual and overestimating recurrence

Every multivariate odds ratio rests on 11-13 events against 5-6 covariates, producing confidence intervals spanning an order of magnitude (1.088-16.387; 1.760-24.820; 1.005-17.128; 1.599-28.057). These are unstable estimates from overfitted models, and the margin result (p = 0.048) and the thermal ablation result (p = 0.048, lower CI limit 1.005) sit exactly at the significance boundary

Variables entering the multivariate models were preselected on univariate significance in a 106-patient dataset, which inflates the apparent effect of whichever variable survives and is why the two recurrence models produce opposite risk factors with no interaction or formal comparison between them

The protective effect attributed to pancreatic stenting is confounded by indication in the reverse direction: stents were placed in 73.6% at the endoscopist's discretion, and the cases where stenting was omitted are plausibly those with difficult anatomy or bleeding - the same conditions that predispose to pancreatitis

Only 1 of 106 index resections was judged incomplete endoscopically (99.1% complete) while 20.8% had positive or uncertain margins and 10.4% had adenoma at the first surveillance - so endoscopic assessment of completeness was essentially uninformative, which undercuts 'curative resection' and 'endoscopic success' as defined (both rest partly on a negative visual margin)

Margins were simplified to positive-or-uncertain versus negative because centres did not record vertical and lateral separately; that pools 19 genuinely positive with 3 uncertain margins and loses exactly the distinction that the companion Korean study (Yoon 2023) found to carry prognostic weight

The statement that hospital setting and endoscopist experience did not affect outcomes is presented as a finding, but all five centres performed over 500 ERCPs/year with operators of more than 5 years' experience - the range tested is too narrow to detect a volume effect, so this is a null comparison between similar practices rather than evidence that volume is irrelevant

Mean follow-up 36.2 months with a 1-year minimum means late recurrence beyond 3 years is largely unobserved; the paper notes the longest adenoma-free interval before recurrence was 27 months, which is less than the 9.75 years reported in a companion series, so the 12.3% late recurrence is a floor
Adenocarcinoma was found in 4 final specimens and these patients remain in the denominator for curative resection and recurrence, mixing a different disease into an adenoma outcome series

Inferring that EUS cannot predict persistence because both re-recurrence-to-surgery patients had EUS is an argument from 2 patients in a cohort where EUS was performed in only a third, at the operator's discretion
35633905.n: 106 patients (from 119 collected) after excluding 7 with inadequate follow-up and 6 with non-adenomatous lesions; mean age 61.4 years, 62 men; mean follow-up 36.2 months (SD 18.3); seven endoscopists with more than 5 years of ERCP experience at centres performing over 500 ERCPs/year
35633905.bottom_line: In 106 patients from five Korean tertiary centres, endoscopic papillectomy achieved curative resection in 76% and avoided surgery in 93%, with a positive/uncertain margin predicting early recurrence and piecemeal resection predicting late recurrence and non-curative resection - a useful distinction, but one drawn from 11-13 events with very wide confidence intervals, inconsistent reported denominators, and a recurrence classification that depends on surveillance timing rather than biology.
35633905.funding: National Research Foundation of Korea grants NRF-2021M3E5D1A01015177 (Korean Government) and NRF-2018R1D1A1B07048202 (Ministry of Education); authors declare no conflict of interest

limitations: Case numbers are too small to identify statistically significant differences between the MMR-deficient and MMR-proficient subsets, or between TPS- and CPS-positive cases

PD-L1 cut-offs and scoring criteria had to be extrapolated from non-small cell lung and gastric cancer because none are established for ampullary carcinoma, and thresholds and antibodies remain in flux
MLH1 promoter methylation testing was performed in only one case, so the Lynch association can only be suggested; testing the remaining cases would be needed to confirm it
A clinical trial is needed before immunotherapy can be recommended on the basis of these findings
critique: Eleven cases is not a cohort for survival comparison: with 3 deaths the reported 5-year survival of 53% has no meaningful precision, and the paper's suggestion that medullary carcinoma 'may be less aggressive' rests on a non-significant difference of 6 percentage points (p = 0.47) that the discussion nonetheless escalates to 'the prognosis of MC appears to be more favorable'

The MMR comparison is between all 11 medullary cases and only 119 of 348 non-medullary cases that happened to have been tested, a convenience denominator from a separate publication; if testing was ordered preferentially for suspicious morphology the 15% background rate is inflated and the odds ratio understated, or vice versa

Medullary morphology was assigned without any blinded review or interobserver agreement data, despite the authors' own citation of published interobserver variability in diagnosing colorectal medullary carcinoma and their group's demonstration that ampullary subtyping is only fairly reproducible

PD-L1 was assessed in 8 of 11 cases, EBV in 3, INI1 in 8 and methylation in 1, with no statement of why the others lacked tissue; selective availability of material for the markers that generate the therapeutic claim is a real risk of bias
The headline that PD-L1 positivity is independent of MMR status comes from 4 MMR-proficient tumours, of which 3 were CPS positive - a result fully compatible with chance

No adjuvant treatment data are reported for either group, so the survival comparison cannot be interpreted; 'MC should be considered for targeted therapy' is an inference from staining frequency with no outcome data behind it

Describing the 64% MMR-deficiency rate as grounds for stronger testing is reasonable, but the single Lynch case does not support the stated 'high potential for Lynch association' in the absence of germline testing in the other six deficient cases

A 24-year accrual window (1989-2013) with no stated change in pathology practice means the 3% frequency depends on retrospective re-reading of decades-old slides against a criterion (50% non-gland-forming) adopted from a 2021 CAP protocol
36502926.n: 11 medullary carcinomas (3%) among 359 invasive ampullary carcinomas; PD-L1 assessed in 8, INI1 in 8, EBV in 3; comparator group 348 non-medullary ampullary carcinomas (MMR tested in 119)
36502926.bottom_line: Establishes medullary carcinoma as a recognisable 3% subset of ampullary cancer that is strongly MMR-deficient, BRAF wild-type and almost uniformly PD-L1 positive regardless of MMR status, which justifies routine MMR testing; it does not establish that these tumours behave less aggressively or that immunotherapy benefits them.
36502926.funding: Not stated; disclosures declared as none

limitations: Retrospective design, which the authors argue is mitigated by propensity score matching that successfully balanced baseline features
The authors state a prospective study is ethically difficult, especially in adenocarcinoma, because patients would have to accept the risk of missing an opportunity for radical resection
The low incidence of advanced ampullary adenoma makes an adequately powered single-centre study impossible, which is why a multicentre national cohort was used
critique: The conclusion that papillectomy alone is non-inferior rests on a 55-patient matched comparison in which recurrence-free survival was 66.1% versus 86.7% with p = 0.052. A 20-point absolute difference that misses significance in a tiny sample is not evidence of equivalence, and the subgroup with cancer shows the same pattern (61.4% vs 82.6%, p = 0.066). The paper presents two near-misses in the same direction as reassurance

Matching discarded 72 of 94 papillectomy-alone patients to find 22 matches for 33 surgical patients - a 1:n nearest-neighbour match within 0.05 that inverted the usual ratio and left the smaller arm as the exposure of interest. Post-matching the groups still differed on adenocarcinoma proportion (63.6% vs 75.8%) and the paper reports no standardised mean differences or balance diagnostics

Treatment allocation was by the treating physician on exactly the variables that predict outcome - margin positivity and adenocarcinoma - and matching on those variables cannot remove the unmeasured clinical judgement (frailty, comorbidity, patient refusal) that also drove the decision. Patients who were too unwell for surgery are pooled with patients deliberately surveilled

Immortal time bias is unaddressed: the surgery group had to survive and remain fit for up to 3 months after papillectomy to enter that arm, while the papillectomy-alone arm includes anyone who did not, which biases overall survival in favour of surgery and against the paper's own conclusion - yet no landmark analysis is performed

T stage is never reported. In a cohort where a quarter to three-quarters of patients have adenocarcinoma, the absence of any T1a/T1b distinction makes the result uninterpretable, since T1b carries a substantially higher nodal metastasis risk and the whole clinical question turns on that split

Nodal status is unknown for the papillectomy-alone arm by definition (no lymphadenectomy), so comparing survival against a surgically staged arm compares groups with different information, and 'recurrence' in the unstaged arm depends entirely on how diligently CT and endoscopy were performed

Surveillance after the index inspection was left to each institution's policy, with only a floor of endoscopy twice yearly and CT annually across 9 hospitals, so recurrence ascertainment is non-uniform between arms and centres

Margin information was missing for 10 of 33 surgical patients and the margin categories include 'positive without further information' (8 surgery, 1 papillectomy) and 'uncertain' (5 papillectomy) - so the margin analysis that generates the paper's actionable recommendation is built on an incompletely classified variable

The margin-survival analysis is a within-arm comparison across four categories in 94 patients, reported only as log-rank p values with no hazard ratios, no adjustment for histology or tumour size, and no correction for multiple comparisons across four margin groups and two endpoints

The diagnostic concordance table, which is the paper's most robust contribution, is drawn from 485 papillectomies but the survival analysis uses only 127 of them; the two parts of the paper therefore describe different populations and the concordance figures cannot be used to characterise the survival cohort
Median follow-up 43.3 months is used to report 5-year survival, so the headline estimates are extrapolations beyond the observed data in both arms
36587061.n: 127 patients with high-grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma after endoscopic papillectomy (94 papillectomy alone, 33 subsequent surgery) drawn from 485 papillectomies within a cohort of 1607 ampullary tumour patients; matched cohort 55 (22 papillectomy alone, 33 surgery); median follow-up 43.3 months
36587061.bottom_line: In a Korean multicentre cohort, patients whose papillectomy specimen showed high-grade dysplasia or adenocarcinoma had similar overall survival whether or not they went on to radical surgery, and margin status - particularly both margins positive - identified those who did badly; but the recurrence-free survival difference favoured surgery at p = 0.052 in only 55 matched patients, T stage is never reported, and allocation was driven by the same variables used for matching.
36587061.funding: A grant from the Korean Society of Gastrointestinal Cancer Research (2021); authors declare no conflict of interest or financial ties

limitations: Retrospective single-institution design may introduce selection bias despite the 10-year window at a tertiary academic centre
Many cases lack follow-up biopsy or resection pathology, so the concordance and discordance rates reflect only the cases that had follow-up
critique: The denominator problem the authors mention is fatal to the headline numbers: concordance is computed on 90 of 252 patients (36%), and the patients who went on to resection are precisely those whose biopsy or clinical picture raised concern, so the 8.9% major discrepancy rate is a lower bound on the false-negative rate that could be far higher in the unresected 64%

Sensitivity of 60% for biopsy and 89% for combined biopsy plus cytology is calculated on 20 and 9 cases respectively; no confidence intervals are given, and with 9 cases the combined estimate could as easily be 50% as 99%

The 'combined biopsy and cytology improves sensitivity' recommendation is confounded by indication: cytology was ordered in 88% of periampullary but 17% of ampullary tumours, i.e. precisely for deep-seated lesions where biopsy was expected to fail, so the incremental yield of cytology is not estimable from these data
Three of five pathologists knew the malignant cytology result before signing out the biopsy, so the biopsy diagnoses are not independent of the comparator used to judge them

Assigning 7 of 8 false negatives to 'sampling limitation' rather than interpretive error is a retrospective judgement by the same authors who signed out some of the cases, with no blinded re-review or second-reader adjudication; the one error they did identify was found only because DOG-1 was run retrospectively, which suggests the method would not detect interpretive misses in glandular lesions

The resected series collapses true ampullary (12), distal bile duct (6), pancreatic (1) and GIST (1) tumours into one narrative, so stage and nodal statements mix entities the companion literature insists must be kept apart

No interobserver reproducibility data for the dysplasia grading that generates 27 of the 35 discordances, although the paper cites published intraobserver and interobserver variability in exactly this setting
The p53 immunostain recommended as a practical aid is described from local practice with no accuracy data from this cohort
37595391.n: 318 ampullary biopsy specimens from 252 patients, with 169 follow-up biopsy/resection specimens available for 90 patients; 21 resected cases analysed clinicopathologically
37595391.bottom_line: Confirms with institutional data that a benign ampullary biopsy does not exclude malignancy - almost 9% of biopsies with follow-up were benign where the resection showed cancer, nearly all from sampling limitation - and suggests combining biopsy with cytology, but the estimates come from the third of patients who had follow-up pathology and the cytology comparison is confounded by indication.

limitations: Retrospective single-centre tertiary care experience, limiting generalisability
Identifying recurrence remains technically challenging even with narrow band imaging and high-definition white light, particularly intraductal recurrence

Follow-up was not uniform and the mean duration was only 2.8 years; because an uptick in recurrence may occur after 4 years and not all patients were followed that long, the results may underestimate the true recurrence rate
Given the low number of recurrences, identification of risk factors was underpowered
All procedures were performed by endoscopists with substantial ERCP experience, and papillectomy carries an ASGE level 4 complexity rating, further limiting generalisability
critique: The internal arithmetic does not add up: the abstract reports 20 recurrences, but the en bloc versus piecemeal breakdown gives 13 plus 4 (17), and the complete versus residual breakdown gives 15 plus 2 (17). Three recurrences are unaccounted for in both stratifications, so the denominators behind the comparisons cannot be verified

The paper's central claim about timing is stated two different ways: the abstract says 9 of 20 recurrences (45%) occurred after the first 2 years of surveillance, while the discussion says 'nearly half the recurrences occurred after 3 years of surveillance' and that the probability of recurrence 'experienced a leap 4 years after papillectomy'. The Kaplan-Meier table shows no events in year 4 at all, so the narrative does not match the data

Recurrence counts by resection type run counter to every other series and to the paper's own framing: 19.4% after en bloc versus 7.0% after piecemeal resection, and 16.5% after initially complete versus 6.1% after residual-tissue resection. These are reported without comment, but they are the signature of detection bias - patients with piecemeal or residual disease were scoped more intensively early, had their lesions re-treated, and so were classified as residual rather than recurrent

That classification is the deeper problem: by requiring one negative surveillance endoscopy before an event counts as recurrence, and by allowing multiple treatment sessions within 'complete eradication', the study converts early incomplete resection into non-events and shifts the apparent recurrence curve rightwards - which is precisely the direction needed to argue for longer surveillance

With 20 events and 13 candidate variables, the Cox model is severely overfitted; every adjusted hazard ratio is below 1.4 with intervals spanning 0.1 to 7.7, so the finding that 'no variables predicted recurrence' is uninformative rather than reassuring, as the authors concede

Mean follow-up of 2.8 years against a mean time to recurrence of 3.2 years means more than half the person-time needed to observe the events being described was never accumulated; the 5-year cumulative estimate of 14.5% rests on a thin tail, and the recommendation to extend surveillance to 10 years is driven by a single outlier recurrence at 9.75 years

The 18-year accrual window spans the introduction of high-definition endoscopy, narrow band imaging, radiofrequency ablation and routine rectal NSAIDs (given to only 26.5% of this cohort), so technique, detection sensitivity and complication risk all changed within the cohort, and no era analysis is presented

21 patients with adenocarcinoma are pooled into an adenoma recurrence series; only 12 of them entered the recurrence analysis, and 2 recurred with adenocarcinoma - events with entirely different clinical meaning from an adenoma recurrence, counted in the same rate

The FAP comparison that contradicts the much-cited 58% recurrence figure from Ma et al. is based on 35 FAP patients with a shorter follow-up than that study, and the authors acknowledge this, yet the abstract-level message ('recurrence rate did not differ by baseline pathology') invites readers to drop FAP-specific surveillance

Adverse events of 27.2% including 4.8% perforation and 2.2% severe pancreatitis are higher than in most comparator series in this depot, but are reported without any analysis of predictors or era, and are not weighed against the recurrence findings in the conclusion

Follow-up data were supplemented by telephone calls to patients, an ascertainment method that cannot confirm histological recurrence and introduces differential completeness between patients still attending the centre and those lost to it

Several authors declare consultancies with endoscope and device manufacturers (Boston Scientific, Olympus, Cook, Medtronic) in a paper whose conclusion is to extend endoscopic surveillance to 10 years
38015261.n: 165 papillectomies screened, 136 patients with adenomatous pathology analysed (mean age 61.9, SD 15; 70 women, 51.5%; mean lesion size 21.2 mm, SD 12); 124 (91.2%) achieved complete eradication and entered the recurrence analysis with 345.8 person-years of follow-up (mean 2.8 years per patient, SD 3.3)
38015261.bottom_line: Reports a 16.1% recurrence rate (5.8 per 100 person-years) after endoscopic papillectomy with recurrences occurring as late as 9.75 years and roughly half after the recommended 2-year surveillance window, which supports longer follow-up; but the event counts are internally inconsistent, the mean follow-up (2.8 years) is shorter than the mean time to recurrence (3.2 years), and the counter-intuitive finding of more recurrence after en bloc and after initially complete resection points to detection bias in how residual disease was classified.
38015261.funding: NIH T32DK007038 (SH). Multiple author disclosures: advisory board membership and consultancies with Boston Scientific, Olympus, Cook Medical, Medtronic, Cernostics, Exact Sciences and Interpace, and research funding from Lucid, Ambu and CDx.

limitations: Retrospective design in which selection bias and missing data cannot be definitively excluded, mitigated by requiring consecutive inclusion and by the matched analysis
No formal study monitoring was possible because of limited resources, and monitoring of cases not included during the study period was not possible
Both low- and high-volume centres were included and centre volume was not analysed, which the authors defend as better reflecting daily practice
Excluding patients with missing data could itself introduce selection bias, although an exclusion analysis showed those patients were comparable on age, sex, comorbidities and lesion size

Recurrence can only be reliably excluded by careful endoscopy with routine biopsy even when macroscopy is normal, and such detailed data are not available in a large retrospective database, so later recurrences cannot be excluded
The reported 16% recurrence after histologic R0 means complete resection should be interpreted with caution

Submucosal injection, used in 24.2% of matched papillectomy patients, is no longer recommended by ESGE but was permitted by the original database criteria and could have influenced the endoscopic results
The study was not designed to analyse survival
Lesions beyond 30 mm could not be evaluated because too few were available in the matched cohorts

A randomised trial would give the highest level of evidence but is judged unrealistic: a two-armed trial would need 190 randomised patients (95 per group, alpha 0.05, power 0.95, effect size 0.5) and with an estimated 30% dropout a screening population of 315 patients with ampullary lesions, and surgical ampullectomy is not broadly available
critique: The matched comparison is almost entirely one-sided in construction: the 62 matched pairs represent 98.4% of the eligible surgical patients but only 10.9% of the eligible papillectomy patients, so the surgical arm is its whole population while the endoscopic arm is a 1-in-9 selection chosen to resemble it. Any residual difference in the matched analysis reflects which papillectomy patients could be matched, not a balanced contrast

Matching omitted the variables that most obviously drove the choice of procedure and the chance of R0: intraductal extension, bile and pancreatic duct dilation, and the use of concomitant ablation (patients ablated at the index papillectomy were deliberately excluded from matching). Table 4 shows intrabiliary extension on imaging and duct dilation still differed significantly after matching (21% vs 8.1%, p = 0.01; 45.2% vs 30.6%, p = 0.001), so confounding by indication survives the propensity model

Follow-up was more than twice as long in the surgical arm in both cohorts (37.5 vs 15.5 months after matching), which biases the recurrence comparison - the paper's clearest finding - against the endoscopic arm's apparent advantage and in favour of the surgical arm's 3.2%; a recurrence rate cannot be compared between arms observed for different durations without a time-to-event analysis, and none is presented for recurrence

Conversely, surveillance intensity was asymmetric in the other direction: endoscopic patients were routinely scoped with biopsies of the scar while surgical patients were not systematically re-scoped, so the fivefold recurrence difference conflates true residual disease with differential ascertainment. The authors acknowledge recurrence 'much depends on the scrutiny of follow-up' but still attribute the difference to the deeper resection plane of ampullectomy

The surgical arm has 63 patients and 6 cancers. Every surgical subgroup statement - 66.6% R0 in cancer (4 of 6), 92.9% R0 in adenoma (53 of 57), 3.2% recurrence (2 of 63) - rests on single-digit numerators, and the only procedure-related death also sits in that arm, so the safety comparison (1.9% vs 3.2%, p = 0.38) has no power at all to detect the morbidity difference that drives the clinical choice

23.2% of the 1673 eligible datasets were excluded for missing or inconclusive data and a further 652 for clinical reasons, leaving 40% of papillectomies and 25% of ampullectomies. The exclusion analysis compares only age, sex, comorbidities and lesion size - not stage, margin or outcome - so it cannot rule out that outcome-related data were differentially missing

The R0 definition is applied to specimens handled by local pathologists at 58 centres over 14 years with no central review, no interobserver assessment and no standard protocol; given that the adjacent literature shows 26% of en bloc papillectomy specimens cannot even be margin-assessed, R0 is being compared between a fragmented endoscopic specimen and an intact surgical one, which structurally favours surgery independent of oncological completeness

Attributing additional ablation at the index procedure to presumed visible residual tissue and therefore reclassifying it as R2 is a reasonable assumption, but it is an assumption made retrospectively by the authors; the 65.9% figure that results is then used as the real papillectomy success rate, and both 80.2% and 65.9% appear in the paper without a single preferred estimate

T1a and T1b cancers are pooled in most analyses despite the authors noting these carry significantly different nodal metastasis risk, and the 13 T1b patients treated endoscopically are precisely the group in whom local resection is most questionable

The matched-cohort severe complication counts are 1 versus 2 events, yet the paper concludes 'both procedures were safe'; with these numbers a two- or threefold difference in serious morbidity would be undetectable

Overall survival is reported as comparable in a study the authors concede was not designed to analyse survival, with median follow-up 21 months in a disease whose resected median survival exceeds 4 years - the survival curves carry essentially no information and should not be used to support equivalence

Procedures spanning 2007-2020 include the pre-ESGE-guideline era, submucosal injection in a quarter of matched endoscopic cases, and the introduction of endobiliary radiofrequency ablation; no era stratification is performed despite technique having changed materially
39642968.n: From 2862 patients in the ESAP database (1189 pancreatoduodenectomies excluded first), 1673 remained (1422 papillectomy, 251 surgical ampullectomy); after exclusions 569 papillectomy (40.0% of database papillectomies) and 63 surgical ampullectomy (25.1%) were analysed, with 62 matched pairs; median follow-up 21 months (IQR 10-47)
39642968.bottom_line: The largest comparison of endoscopic papillectomy with transduodenal surgical ampullectomy shows that a third of procedures in both arms were done for the wrong indication (non-neoplastic histology or advanced cancer), that surgery achieves higher initial R0 (90% vs 73%) with far lower recurrence after R0 (3.2% vs 16%) but at 7 times the procedure time and 11 extra hospital days, and that papillectomy fails in two-thirds of T1 cancers; but the matched analysis pairs the entire surgical population with a 1-in-9 selection of endoscopic patients, follow-up was twice as long in the surgical arm, and surveillance intensity differed, so the recurrence gap is inflated by design.

limitations: Retrospective multi-institutional data with the usual biases; overall statistical power remained low because of disease rarity despite multiple centres
The small sample prevented splitting into derivation and validation cohorts, so the proposed score has not undergone formal validation
Ampullary lesions were not separated from duodenal lesions involving the periampullary region, although no outcome difference was found between them
Not every patient was tested genetically for FAP, MUTYH-associated polyposis or other mutations, though all underwent colonoscopy and family history assessment

Sampling bias is acknowledged because the cohort consists only of non-FAP periampullary adenomas that went on to pancreatoduodenectomy; the high malignancy rate reflects selection of high-risk cases by tumour size and location, and the true denominator - including patients managed by endoscopic mucosal resection or transduodenal resection - is unclear
A prospective study to identify the true denominator may not be feasible given the low incidence
critique: The three risk strata are reported with mutually inconsistent numbers: the abstract gives low risk n = 26, intermediate n = 59, high n = 26 with rates 10.3%, 44.1% and 88.2%; the results text gives 11.5%, 41.7% and 84.6%; Table 4 gives 3/29, 26/59 and 30/34. Three different sets of denominators for the paper's central output means the score's calibration cannot be verified from the published data

The score was derived and evaluated in the same 127 patients with no split-sample, bootstrap or cross-validation, no c-statistic, no calibration plot and no sensitivity or specificity at any threshold. An OR of 77.5 for the high-risk group (CI 15.9-375.9) is the signature of an in-sample fit, and the paper's own concession that validation was impossible should preclude clinical use

The denominator problem the authors acknowledge is fatal to the score's intended purpose: everyone in the cohort had a Whipple, so the score is calibrated on the subset already judged to need resection. A patient weighing resection against endoscopic surveillance is by definition outside this population, and applying a 46% baseline malignancy rate to them would badly overestimate risk - exactly the misuse the shared-decision framing invites

Two of the four score components are proxies for obstruction, not for neoplastic progression: 'any preoperative symptom' (worth 2 points) is a list including fatigue, nausea and dark urine, and common bile duct dilation of 9 mm or more. Jaundice and biliary stenting were dropped from the model as redundant with symptoms, which concedes the point - the score largely measures whether the lesion is obstructing, and the discussant at the meeting objected that a jaundiced patient with no other factor scores only 1-2

The inverse complication relationship is presented as a feature of the score but has a simpler explanation the paper does not address: patients with benign pathology had soft, non-atrophic glands and non-dilated ducts because they had no obstructing cancer, and fistula risk follows gland texture and duct size. Adjusting for duct size and texture in the final model does not remove this, because the same obstruction physiology that lowers fistula risk is what the score is detecting

The complication finding only becomes significant after the three prespecified strata are collapsed at score 3 - across the strata as defined it was non-significant (p = 0.11) with the intermediate and high groups indistinguishable (27.1% vs 29.4%). Choosing the dichotomy that yields p = 0.047 after the three-group comparison failed is a post hoc cut-point

Preoperative dysplasia grade carries 2 of the 6 points but was read by local pathologists at 8 centres over 12 years, with no central review and no interobserver data - and the invited discussants specifically questioned whether a pathologist seeing roughly one such case per year can reliably separate high- from low-grade dysplasia

Volume was extremely low: 127 patients across 8 institutions over 12 years, about 1.3 cases per centre per year, so biopsy technique, number of biopsies, prior attempted endoscopic resection and pathology interpretation almost certainly varied in ways that cannot be modelled - a point the discussants raised and the authors do not rebut with data

EUS findings are absent from the entire paper despite both discussants noting that these are major centres where EUS would be routine; omitting the modality that best assesses intraductal extension and depth from a preoperative risk score is a substantial gap, and no explanation is given

Lesion size was missing for 27 of 127 patients (21%) and was then excluded from the score on the grounds that it did not differ between groups - a conclusion drawn from data with a fifth missing and no imputation

Black race was associated with benign final pathology (26.5% vs 11.9%) and with a different risk profile, in a cohort where race also tracked with symptoms and stenting; no analysis addresses whether differential access to earlier endoscopic diagnosis is embedded in the score's components

The 46.4% malignancy rate is compared with the same group's earlier single-centre figure of 29%, with no explanation for the difference other than cohort composition - which again points to the selection the score cannot escape
39831703.n: 127 patients of 189 reviewed; median age 65 years (34-89), 57 men (44.9%); 82 (64.6%) preoperative duodenal adenoma and 45 (35.4%) ampullary adenoma, with ampullary involvement in 84 of 119 (70.6%); 59 (46.4%) had malignancy on final pathology
39831703.bottom_line: Confirms in the largest surgical series that nearly half of sporadic periampullary adenomas taken to pancreatoduodenectomy harbour cancer and that patients with benign final pathology paradoxically suffer threefold more major complications, and proposes a 0-6 malignancy risk score from age, bile duct diameter, symptoms and high-grade dysplasia; but the score is derived and tested in the same 127 already-resected patients with no validation, its published strata carry three inconsistent sets of numbers, and two of its four components are proxies for biliary obstruction.

limitations: The Delphi methodology, while the best option for reaching consensus, carries the difficulty of capturing all key issues in the literature during questionnaire development, depends on panellists' ongoing willingness to participate, and risks skewed data because those less confident about a topic may not participate

Although the stated aim was to cover all non-pancreatic cancers of the periampullary region, more recommendations relate to ampullary cancer than to common bile duct or duodenal cancer; the authors accept this imbalance as reflecting greater uncertainty and need for guidance about ampullary cancer

For a considerable proportion of the consensus questions there are fairly limited published data, so most recommendations are supported only by a low level of evidence, which the authors say highlights the early stage of knowledge about periampullary cancer

The authors state that the lack of consensus definitions and standardisation, together with high interobserver variability, has hindered consistent conclusions across studies - particularly regarding patient management including the efficacy of adjuvant chemotherapy, which remains highly controversial because of these inconsistencies
critique: Almost every recommendation is graded low level of evidence with a weak form of recommendation, or rests on expert opinion alone. This is honest, but it means a document that will be used to standardise reporting worldwide is in substance a codification of the opinions of 43 experts, most of them from the pathology study groups that initiated it

THE PROCESS METRICS PROMISED ARE NOT REPORTED. The methods describe an independent Jury Committee calculating a 'Quality Score' using the AGREE II tool across 23 items and six domains, and an audience vote on each recommendation at the Brescia meeting. Neither result appears anywhere in the paper - no AGREE II score, no domain breakdown, no audience agreement percentages. The quality-assurance apparatus is described but its findings are withheld

The Delphi convergence is itself a weak signal: 33 of 57 recommendations reached 80% agreement in round one and the rest were revised by the responsible expert team according to the dissenting comments and re-voted until they passed. Revising a statement until it achieves consensus guarantees consensus; the final 50 of 51 figure measures iteration, not agreement on the original propositions

The 30% threshold for calling a tumour 'mixed' subtype has no stated derivation. It is a cut-point that will determine subtype assignment in a large fraction of cases - and the consensus itself cites that about 40% of ampullary carcinomas are mixed - yet no data, reproducibility study or sensitivity analysis is offered for choosing 30% over 10% or 50%

Renaming the hybrid category 'tubular-NOS' is a nomenclature change, not a solution. The underlying problem documented in this depot - that five pathologists agree on morphological subtype at kappa 0.39 with full agreement in 23% of cases - is unaddressed: no interobserver reproducibility study of the new definitions is reported or planned, so the consensus standardises the words without demonstrating that the categories can be applied consistently

The consensus states plainly that the prognostic and predictive role of subtype is unclear because of inconsistent historical definitions, yet it simultaneously retains subtyping as a required element of the pathology report and advises subtyping on biopsy where subtype 'may affect treatment'. If subtype has no established treatment implication, there is no situation in which that condition is met

Reflex MMR testing is recommended on the grounds that prevalence is 'comparable to that of colorectal cancer and is also independent on the subtype', but the supporting evidence is graded low and the two papers in this depot give prevalences of 15% in unselected non-medullary ampullary carcinoma and 4.3% in early-onset ampullary cancer - neither of which is clearly comparable to colorectal, and neither of which is cited as a prevalence estimate in the recommendation

Tumour budding is recommended as prognostically stronger than T stage and nodal metastasis, a strong empirical claim resting largely on work from the same institutional tradition that produced the ampullary classifications, with no multi-institutional validation, no reproducibility data for the 3-foci-per-200x-field threshold, and the acknowledged problem that biopsies may not contain the invasive front where budding must be assessed

229 of 37061 screened articles (0.6%) were selected, with allocation of articles to anonymous expert teams but no stated inclusion criteria, no risk-of-bias appraisal of the 229, no PRISMA flow diagram in the main text and no evidence tables - so the SIGN framework is invoked without the apparatus that makes it auditable

The anatomic definitions, which are the document's most valuable contribution, are operationalised in terms of tumour 'epicentre' and 'minimal involvement' without quantitative thresholds except in the earlier Adsay scheme they derive from; given that this literature's own data show that 21% of cases labelled ampullary are reclassified on strict review, the definitions need a reproducibility study more than they need wider adoption

The panel is heavily weighted towards pathology (initiated by ISGACA with ISGPP as steering committee), and the multidisciplinary part generated only 17 of 51 recommendations; the oncological questions that clinicians most need settled - whether subtype should guide adjuvant therapy, what to do with a T1 cancer after papillectomy - are declared unresolved rather than addressed

The consensus correctly identifies that inconsistent definitions have made the adjuvant chemotherapy literature uninterpretable, which is the strongest argument in this depot against acting on the Bolm-versus-Ecker dispute; but it stops at saying standardised future studies are needed and offers no interim guidance
40729532.bottom_line: The first international consensus to define precisely what counts as ampullary carcinoma, to retire the term 'periampullary' as a diagnosis, to set a 30% threshold for the mixed subtype and rename the hybrid group 'tubular-NOS', to make mismatch repair testing reflex, and to state explicitly that the prognostic and predictive value of intestinal-versus-pancreatobiliary subtype remains unclear because the historical literature used inconsistent definitions - which is the key caveat for any pathway claiming subtype should guide adjuvant therapy; but almost every recommendation is low-evidence or expert opinion, the promised AGREE II quality score and audience vote are never reported, and no reproducibility study accompanies the new definitions.
40729532.funding: Amsterdam Gastroenterology Endocrinology Metabolism (AGEM), Amsterdam, The Netherlands; the authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: Retrospective design over a 10-year period across 22 institutions, which may introduce missing data and selection bias

Treatment strategies - papillectomy technique, surveillance intervals and argon plasma coagulation use - varied by institution and over time because standardised guidelines were not consistently available; the authors stratified analysis by treatment period to address this
Only high-volume centres with expert teams were included, limiting generalisability
R0 margin status was assessed locally at each institution rather than centrally, which may introduce variability, although recurrence rates after R0 were comparable to other large studies
T1a and T1b adenocarcinomas were not differentiated, so prognosis by tumour stage could not be examined
critique: The hazard ratios differ between the abstract/discussion and Table 2 for the same comparisons (Rx 2.30 [1.44-3.68] versus 2.38 [1.49-3.81]; R1 2.95 [1.85-4.71] versus 2.95 [1.87-4.66]). The discrepancy is small but it means two different models or datasets were in play and neither is identified

The central finding - recurrence after R0 - is partly a definitional artefact of Japanese pathological practice, which the paper itself flags: non-invasive intraepithelial neoplasia is diagnosed as carcinoma in Japan but as high-grade dysplasia in the West, so 'adenocarcinoma' in the 92 cases here is not equivalent to adenocarcinoma in the Western series alongside it, and the adenocarcinoma hazard ratio cannot be transferred

Recurrence is defined as histologic confirmation of neoplastic tissue with no requirement for a prior negative surveillance endoscopy, and the median time to recurrence was 6 months (3 months after R1). That makes a large fraction of 'recurrences' residual disease, as the pattern by margin status shows - which is consistent but means the 18.3% figure is not comparable with series that excluded residual disease, including Han 2024 in this same depot

The later treatment era (2015-2020) independently predicted recurrence (HR 1.57), which the authors attribute to more procedures by operators with fewer than 20 prior cases (26.4% rising to 44.0%). Since operator experience was not itself significant, this is an unexplained period effect that could equally reflect intensified surveillance in later years - a detection artefact that would inflate the headline recurrence rate

Margin assessment was local across 22 centres with no central pathology review and no interobserver data, yet R0/R1/Rx is the paper's principal exposure; a quarter of the cohort was Rx precisely because margins could not be read, and Rx behaved almost identically to R1 at 5 years (34% each), suggesting Rx is largely undetected R1

The R0 subgroup analysis generates the paper's most quotable new risk factors from very few events, with wildly unstable estimates: argon plasma coagulation HR 6.26 (1.44-27.1) rests on 69 of 396 R0 patients having received APC, and bile duct invasion HR 4.86 (1.08-21.8) on a handful of cases. The authors correctly reinterpret APC as a marker of endoscopically suspected residual disease rather than a cause, but the abstract-level framing does not carry that caveat

The pancreatic duct invasion estimate is reported as 0.00 (0.00-infinity) - a non-estimate from a zero cell - and is then used to argue that bile duct but not pancreatic duct invasion matters, an inference the data cannot support

Patients censored at 5 years and 21 patients removed for post-papillectomy surgery for residual cancer are exactly the group at highest risk of a bad outcome; removing them from the recurrence denominator while keeping them in the 798-patient resection-status analysis means the two headline numbers (52.1% R0, 18.3% recurrence) have different populations behind them

Female sex emerged as an independent predictor in both models (HR 1.48 and 2.09) with no mechanism offered beyond one prior report; in a model with 13 covariates and 142 events this is as likely to be noise or a proxy for an unmeasured anatomical variable

Follow-up protocols 'varied by center and clinical context' with only a typical interval of 6-12 months stated, so recurrence ascertainment is non-uniform across 22 centres and 12 years - the single most important determinant of a cumulative recurrence estimate is left undocumented

The 32.5% adverse event rate with 19.4% bleeding is substantially higher than most Western series and reflects a Japanese practice of inpatient papillectomy with a 13-day median stay; the paper does not discuss whether this reflects more complete ascertainment or a different complication profile, which matters for anyone comparing the two approaches

Several authors declare lecture fees and research support from endoscope and device manufacturers, and the study was run with the national endoscopy society's guideline committee, in a paper whose conclusions support continued endoscopic surveillance and a redefinition of R0
41192607.n: 875 cases enrolled, 798 with pathologically confirmed ampullary adenoma or adenocarcinoma, 776 in the long-term recurrence analysis (21 excluded for surgery for confirmed or suspected residual adenocarcinoma, 1 for procedure-related death); median age 67 years, 320 women (40.1%), 53 with genetically confirmed FAP (6.6%); median follow-up 33 months (IQR 6.75-60)
41192607.bottom_line: The largest papillectomy cohort to date (798 patients, 22 Japanese centres) shows that histologic R0 is achieved in only half of cases even when en bloc resection looks technically successful, and that recurrence reaches 20% at 3 years overall and still 11% after R0 - so surveillance is needed regardless of margin status; but recurrence here includes early residual disease, the adenocarcinoma category follows Japanese rather than Western criteria, and the R0-subgroup risk factors come from too few events to act on.
